speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: In the same message, the WP committed to tracking how the Government upgrades its legacy schemes for, and I quote: "the circumstances of today and tomorrow, not yesterday".

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The reality of the pressures faced by low- and middle-income Singaporeans was repeated in the WP May Day message that same year.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: And, finally, in our National Day message this year, celebrations which also saw a remake of Dick Lee's 1988 hit, "Home", the WP noted that just as the remake of "Home" comes at a time when Singapore and the world are at a different juncture from a quarter century ago, our national policies also need to be re-examined to make them relevant to today's Singapore.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: On cost of living, the WP acknowledges the one-time reliefs extended to eligible households.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Most recently, on the back of the announcement by the Public Utilities Board (PUB) in late September of an increase in water prices.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: For the purposes of this Motion, the WP will look into possibilities of further reducing cost-of-living pressures by way of policy change.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: This House must leave no stone unturned because, for some Singaporeans, this has become a cost-of-living crisis.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: First, I will cover the situation facing Singaporeans on the ground, particularly for workers, seniors and their families.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Second, I will cover some policy areas where the Government can explore the prospect of lowering costs for Singaporeans in different ways.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: However, from our ground outreach and from feedback received by the WP, cost of living worries for Singaporeans are clearly moving in the opposite direction.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: This is understandable, as there is a chasm between, on the one hand, headlines that say that inflation is stabilising, while on the other hand, price rises continue to hit Singaporeans hard.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The Consumer Price Index (CPI), which measures inflation, only covers household consumption expenditures and does not include non-consumption expenditures, such as loan repayments, the purchase of property, including Housing and Development (HDB) flats, monthly mortgage payments and credit card debt payments.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Interest rates are often accompanied by price increases and loan interest rates remain high.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: What was cash-in-hand not too long ago has, now and in the future, to be used for interest payments.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: This reality reinforces the view that prices are galloping away and that incomes are struggling to catch up.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: It is important to also consider the compounding effect of price increases with costs passed down from enterprises to consumers.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The breadth and depth of the rise in prices also vary considerably, since consumption patterns differ from each household.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: For example, a household with young children will be sensitive to rising tuition and enrichment class costs, in addition to other expenses that accompany raising a child.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Singaporeans who need a vehicle for their work are understandably more sensitive to Certificate of Entitlement (COE), diesel and petrol prices.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: On the other hand, food prices account for a large proportion of income at the lowest strata of society.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: And so, when a plate of chicken rice or noodles goes up by $2 or $3 and coffee prices shoot up far more than increases in water prices, for example, the pinch for low- and even middle-income Singaporeans is real and painful.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: When income growth cannot match this increase in prices, it is perfectly understandable why Singaporeans feel nervous and anxious.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: In some cases, this may even lead to the deterioration of their mental health.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The letter put into words the worries of many Singaporeans that the rising price of goods and services that began right after the COVID-19 crisis would trap Singapore in a vicious circle of unending price increases.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: For example, and I quote: "The transport fare and Goods and Services Tax (GST) increases are likely to trickle down into higher operating costs for all businesses, including hawkers and coffee shop operators, who will then be compelled to pass on the incremental cost by raising their prices to remain profitable and to survive".

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: It goes on: "Life can become challenging and stressful in an inflationary environment with reduced real income and purchasing power.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: One oft-quoted economist expressed surprise at the timing of the announcement of the support package and suggested that the Government was confident of funding it from better-than-expected revenue collected.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: This would explain why it was able to announce the measure halfway through the fiscal year.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: He said, "From a political standpoint, it shows that the overall fiscal position of the Government is strong enough to be able to give some back before the Budget." Sir, this off-Budget package and the Government's current fiscal position calls into question the necessity of a GST hike next year.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The People's Action Party (PAP)'s argument is that a GST hike is necessary and that this is a political decision it has taken for reasons it has explained.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The contributions of the WP in this debate will move beyond one-time fiscal handouts and explore possible structural changes to existing policies to reduce cost-of-living expenses for ordinary Singaporeans who live in an elevated, inflationary and interest-rate environment and they will continue living in such a scenario for some time to come.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Individually, the WP MPs' suggestions will understandably be specific to a particular policy area.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: But taken as a whole, they point to the possibility of instituting significant structural adjustments to policies that account for the reality of today and tomorrow's cost of living environment, especially for low-income groups and those like the sandwich middle class.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: I will now come on to the next part of my speech.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The last time domestic water tariff tiers were restructured, it took place over four years from 1997 to 2000.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: At the end of that exercise, water prices went up more than 120%.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: A major impetus for that price hike was the argument that Singapore would be short of water after the expiry of the 2011 Water Agreement with Malaysia.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: A parallel objective of the exercise was to get Singaporeans to treat water as a precious and strategic resource and to make water conservation a way of life.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Water borne fees were also raised to recover the cost of wastewater treatment.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Prior to the year 2000, the domestic water tariff had three tiers to correspond to different consumption levels.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The three tiers of water prices for domestic use were as follows: households that used zero to 20 cubic metres of water a month followed by those that used 20 to 40 cubic metres and finally, those that used more than 40 cubic metres a month.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: After the water pricing restructuring exercise from the year 2000, the Government did away with three tiers for domestic users and proceeded with only two tiers.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: A household today is charged differently only if it consumes more than 40 cubic metres a month.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: If you consume below 20 cubic metres of water a month, you will be charged at the rate between zero to 40 cubic metres since there is no specific tier between zero and 20 cubic metres of water anymore.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Arising from the changes in the year 2000, the Government decided that it was not going to continue charging households at the lowest rate tier because these households were not subject to a significant water conservation tax.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Based on publicly available information I have perused, there was no argument canvassed for specifically moving away from a three tier to a two-tiered water pricing regime for households beyond general statements of intent, and it was not explained why an increase in the water conservation tax could not be imposed for those consuming between zero and 20 cubic metres of water per month to cohere with treating each drop of water as a precious resource.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: However, arising from the low amount of water conservation tax paid, it was advanced that these households in the lowest domestic tier had little to no incentive to save water.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Prior to the changes of the water pricing structure in 2000, about 56% of Singaporean households used less than 20 cubic metres of water and paid no water conservation tax.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Thirty-four percent if households paid for water at the next tier which was between 20 and 40 cubic metres of water with a low water conservation tax.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The 10% of households that consumed more than 40 cubic metres of water paid a smaller water conservation tax at 15%, than non-domestic consumers at 20%.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The latter was deemed by the Government to be an unsatisfactory state of affairs as large non-domestic water users or businesses were assessed to often recycle a large proportion of the water they used and were not necessarily more wasteful than large domestic users.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The Government argued that the existing pricing structure would jack up business costs and affect Singapore's business costs and competitiveness and will also fail to have a significant effect on smaller households paying lower domestic rates.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The current two-tier compared to the legacy three-tier structure for domestic users does not fairly reflect water consumption patterns.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: In fact, a case can be made that it puts a heavier water conservation tax burden for the majority of users whose overall consumption patterns are already located in the lower half of the current zero to 40 cubic metres end.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: A graduated water conservation tax across the various tiers would incentivise water conservation and continue to serve the policy purpose of ensuring that water is continually treated as a scarce commodity.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: With this more acutely tiered water pricing regime, the quantum of fiscal support provided through GST Vouchers – U-Save can be right-sized proportionately.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Under such a fairer tariff structure, the 96% of households consuming less than 40 cubic metres of water today would be charged a water conservation tax that more progressively reflects how much they actually consumed and these households ought to see a reduction in water charges.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The Government should look into the state of affairs from a fresh perspective and assess if tiers can be introduced for businesses for a fairer and better deployment of the water conservation tax with a view to better support small and medium enterprises (SMEs) that potentially can be incentivised to use less water where possible.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: As public information for the use of water by different types of businesses is not readily available, this would have to be explored further to determine how to make the water conservation tax promote behavioural change for different types of non-domestic users, Introducing tiers for non-domestic consumers would equalise the expectation of water conservation as a shared objective of households and businesses.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: To this end, it would be useful to recap where we were and where we are in our water journey.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Under our Green Plan 2030, Singapore's blueprint for a more sustainable future that sets out our green targets, Singapore aims to reduce household water consumption to 130 litres per person per day.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: As recently as 2017, PUB sought to reduce consumption to 140 litres per person per day by 2030, but the reality of climate change has necessitated the drawing up of new targets.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: I would advance that the lowering the water conservation tax for households that conserve more water under a more finely determined tariff structure would promote behavioural change that would also allow us to meet green targets while simultaneously lowering cost for end consumers.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Moving on to prices more generally, Mr Speaker, the cost of living crisis has not gone unnoticed by Singapore businesses.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Some companies have announced inflation support payments as cost of living subsidies to junior staff.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: But there are companies that have done more than give one-time support.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: For example, Prudential Singapore was reported by The Business Times to have improved medical and outpatient benefits such as dental consultations and outpatient specialist treatments, including alternative treatments.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: These enhancements to existing schemes were in addition to wage adjustments to match inflation and market competitiveness to support employee groups most affected by rising costs.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: DBS Bank, for example, has enhanced the POSB HDB home loan package with an all-in interest rate of 2.6% per annum for borrowers with a monthly income of $2,500 and below.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: In this light, as advanced by the WP, I reiterate the call in this Motion for the Government to review all its existing schemes, make them fit for purpose in this heightened inflationary environment so as to better support Singaporeans against the onslaught of prices, which is destined to continue unabated, particularly with the upcoming hike to the GST.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Take for example the Workforce Income Supplement (WIS) which was extended to workers aged between 30 and 34 last year, including a $200 increase for workers earning a gross income of 2,500 and below.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: If one is self-employed, the cash component of WIS is only 10% with a 90% MediSave contribution.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: As wages traditional do not move was fast and as significant in quantum for Singaporeans at the lower decils, additional cash in hand will provide much needed relief for our workers, sensitive to the needs of the hour.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: A few hundred dollars for seniors who continued to work and for whom WIS payments are pegged at the highest tiers can make a world of difference to their lives.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Arising from a Parliamentary Question (PQ) filed by Ms Hazel Poa in late 2020, we know that individuals aged 85 and above have on average about $6,300 left in their MediSave accounts upon their demise.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: In fact, the aforesaid approach is already taken for the use of MediSave monies with regard to long-term care.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Sengkang GRC MP Louis Chua, He Ting Ru and Jamus Lim will focus on housing, healthcare and transport.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Aljunied GRC MP Gerald Giam will cover public transport, while Sylvia Lim will speak about electricity prices.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: MP for Hougang Single Member Constituency (SMC) Dennis Tan will review certain aspects of means testing in our public healthcare system and help for families with adults with special needs or disabilities.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: For his part, Aljunied GRC MP Faisal Manap will make a case to introduce social protection steps and in the name of a refreshed social compact to adopt a more systematic approach towards tracking the effectiveness of our social assistance programmes.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: We have seen sharp price increases in Europe, the United States (US) and other continents; triggered of by a series of supply shocks that leads to sharp increases in energy, food and commodity prices as well as the demand arising from post-COVID recovery.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: So have the other central banks near and far, raising rates to manage and dampen demand.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Singapore is not spared from this global inflationary crisis.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: While inflation has come down from its peak, households are still having to cope with the impact of the various price increases.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: In addition, we are also faced with domestic cost pressures and, in particular, we are in this necessary transition to uplift the wages of fellow Singaporeans, especially the low-wage workers.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: We can feel firsthand the impact of the cost of living increases in our neighbourhood centres, at our workplaces and in our daily living experiences.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Our low- to middle-income Singaporeans are particularly affected.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: So, what is our counter to these series of rising costs?

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: In the case of Singapore, fortunately, we do have a suite of policy tools that help us mitigate the impact of rising cost pressures.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Our strong Singapore dollar has been an effective broad-based tool to manage imported inflation as almost everything that we consume are imported.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Without the strong Singapore dollar, our inflation and hence, cost of living situation would have been even more severe.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Here, I just want caution that a strong Singapore dollar is not always a given.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: It is not a drop from sky for us.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: We cannot just demand a strong Singapore dollar or decree as such.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: It depends on the markets, which, in turn, depends on whether we have the strong economic fundamentals to deserve this value of the Singapore dollar.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: If our fundamentals are weakened, you can rest assured the markets will find a new value for the Singapore dollar almost instantly.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Fundamentals such as economic dynamism, competent economic management, financial reserves, political stability, social harmony and importantly, prudent fiscal management.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: These factors have a bearing on our international ratings and the confidence in the Singapore dollar and hence, preserve our purchasing power.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: So, let us jealously safeguard this very important asset that we have and not undermine it.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Having a competitive business landscape at both the macro and retail level are important to keep prices in check and to prevent profiteering.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Essentially, we want consumers to have choices and have the option to compare prices, whether it is to choose a new mobile phone plan or to buy groceries from among the supermarkets that we have.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: In Chinese, we call this "货比三家" or "货比或多家", or to be able to compare prices across three or more shops.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Years ago, I was among the strong proponents for the Government to resume building hawker centres and was glad that the Government eventually reversed its policy in 2011 to start building hawker centres again.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Hawker centres, besides keeping our hawker culture going, help to create a competitive environment in the eating house space, directly competing with coffee shops and other eateries.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: More importantly, it offers consumers choices and more value-for-money options.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: We need to keep the business ecosystem competitive, including having diverse sources of supply, just in case we are being outpriced by some of these traditional sources of supply.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Having job and income growth helps an individual and their family cope with the cost of living.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Growing the economy to create good jobs and better pay is critical, which is why we continually invest in skills upgrade to improve employability.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: We need a business-friendly ecosystem and to continually attract investments so as to keep the economy strong and vibrant to create good jobs.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Having a strong economy also helps generate the tax revenues needed to pay for our growing expenditures.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: This is another important component – jobs and income growth.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Beyond the multi-pronged macro strategies, direct Government assistance is the key source of support to help Singaporeans cope with rising costs, both the subsidies and support packages.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: The Government do subsidise substantially in a range of areas – healthcare, housing, education, transport, childcare and a range of social programmes, amongst others.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: To help Singaporeans better cope with the current cost of living concerns and the new GST rates, the Government has provided direct support assistance through the Budget and off-Budget measures since last year.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: We have the permanent GST Voucher scheme and the Assurance Package.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Because of the various enhancements to these packages and the payouts that are spread throughout the year, the Ministry of Finance (MOF) now publishes the calendar view of the monthly disbursements so that it is easier for Singaporeans to anticipate the payouts each month.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: I must say that when I distributed this handout to my residents during a Kopi Talk, all of them welcomed this and kept this so that they can track whether they are receiving all these payouts.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: It is something that is helping our residents directly.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: I believe no government in the world would adopt either extreme approach.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: For that matter, no Town Councils will do that as well.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Rather, we are here debating what that balance is.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: So, we must be prepared that the high-cost situation around the world could worsen or continue for a prolonged period of time.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: In other words, we must be prepared to sustain the long haul.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: For example, in the production of clean water, the higher energy costs to treat and recycle water is an outlay that will flow out of the country to the energy producing country.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: My point here is that we need to be able to always have the means to pay for these costs, which is rising in our current situation.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Just because we freeze prices or put a cap to price increases, the outflow required to pay for these external costs does not just disappear magically.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: This is the only sustainable and sound way forward as we continue to tackle expected and unexpected challenges and crises ahead in this volatile and uncertain world.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Can I have a copy of your amendment?

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: I will allow some time for the copies to be distributed and then ask the Member to move his amendment.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Mr Liang, you can please move your amendment now.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Amendment No 2, "In line 1, to delete 'review its policies so as to' and insert 'continue pursuing policies that together'".

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: It may be convenient that the debate on the original Motion and on any other amendments moved by Members be proceeded with simultaneously as a debate on a single question.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Do I have the hon Members' agreement to this?

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: The question is the amendments as moved by Mr Liang — Yes, Mr Pritam Singh?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: Would the amendments not qualify as a very significant change to the original Motion?

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: So, I think it is still within the ambit of your original Motion.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: However, as a small nation with few natural resources, we are forced to rely on others for our energy needs.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: This leaves us vulnerable to global events, including rising gas prices, tensions in the Middle East and supply disruptions, which all may cause energy prices to spike unexpectedly.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: It is therefore in our national interest to conserve energy and diversify our energy sources.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: This, in turn, will result in higher electricity bills for households and small businesses, adding to the high costs of living that Singaporeans are struggling to grapple with.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: As far as electricity usage is concerned, our priorities should be encouraging energy conservation and managing costs for consumers.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: To this end, I have noted recent Government announcements, such as the setting up of Gasco to centralise gas procurement by next year, which has the potential to bring down the cost of gas for power generation.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: There is also a pilot initiative next year to offer rebates to consumers who reduce usage during peak hours.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: However, in my opinion, more can be done to one, encourage conservation of electricity; and two, lower costs for consumers.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: About 15 years ago, in 2008, this House debated public concerns about high electricity prices.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: At that time, I raised the possibility of adopting a tiered pricing model, which would enable households who consumed moderate amounts of electricity to pay for usage at a lower rate, if their consumption did not exceed a certain threshold.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Households who consumed electricity in excess of the threshold would pay for the excess at a higher rate.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: In rejecting my suggestion in 2008 and again in 2010, then Ministry of Trade and Industry (MTI) Senior Minister of State S Iswaran, argued that the Government intended to facilitate competition in household electricity pricing through opening the retail electricity market.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The Government touted more flexible choices and "competitive pricing" with the new open electricity market for consumers.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Please allow me to quote what then Senior Minister of State Iswaran said: "…in the long term, EMA is working towards opening up the household electricity market for competition so that consumers will be able to purchase electricity direct from different suppliers through a range of retail packages that they offer.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Ms Lim asked whether the Government will allow such retail electricity sellers to use a tiered system.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Once such a market is established, then we should leave it to the market to work out what are the different ways they can meet customer needs...

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: If we were to introduce a tiered system today, it means Government is deciding what is an acceptable level of electricity consumption and establish that as the threshold...

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: This is quite a problematic process in terms of determining the key levels of thresholds.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: So, it would be far superior to allow the market to work, for us to give targeted subsidies to those who need it and when the market is fully liberalised, the players can then work out the schemes as we see in other sectors like telecoms." Sir, it was thus a key plank of the Government's strategy to bank on the open electricity market to manage electricity prices for consumers.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Accordingly, the open electricity market for households was rolled out in 2018, to great fanfare.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Many were under-hedged and were stuck with lower-priced fixed rate electricity contracts while energy prices rose unexpectedly.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: This drove them to a loss-making proposition, leaving them no choice but to exit the market.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Today, most of the remaining retailers are backed by power generation companies while two others offer plans with only "marginal price differences from the regulated tariff".

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: These tighter requirements include requiring a licensee to hedge at least 80% of their contracted retail demand, set up funds to pay for premature termination of contracts and so on.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: A CNA report from August this year observed that these additional requirements could result in higher prices for consumers.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The uptake of price plans from retailers has also been slow.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: According to a report by the Oxford Institute of Energy Studies, barriers to switching in the retail electricity market include complexity of the retail market and electricity tariffs, transaction costs, uncertainty of service quality and behavioural biases, among others.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: There is also the question of how viable it is to have many retailers competing for the relatively small domestic market in Singapore.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: As matters stand now, much uncertainty remains over the revamped open electricity market model.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: It is unclear whether consumers will benefit from the liberalisation of the electricity market and if so, to what extent.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: What, then, are the other options for managing household electricity bills?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: So far, a large part of the Government's answer has been to distribute U-Save vouchers, mainly to HDB households.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: While U-Save vouchers are useful, they are effectively taxpayer subsidies for certain types of households.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: As a complement to these measures, the Government could review its electricity tariff structures.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: In particular, I would ask the Government again to consider implementing a tiered pricing structure for household consumers.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Further or alternatively, the Government should consider a pricing structure that is based on time of use that discourages electricity consumption at peak hours.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Both of these have the potential to lower electricity costs for consumers.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Tiered pricing is known in some countries as increasing block tariffs (IBTs).

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Under such a system, households that consume electricity below a certain threshold would be charged at a lower rate, while those consuming higher amounts would pay higher rates for the excess consumption.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: In 2010, then Senior Minister of State Iswaran responded that tiered pricing would amount to the Government essentially deciding what an "acceptable" level of electricity consumption is.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: What we would be doing is to encourage energy conservation by charging a lower rate for what is deemed a basic necessity.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Tiered pricing of household electricity is used in many countries.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: To understand more about it, we could look to the benefits in several other countries where it has been implemented.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The specific levels differed, depending on the province, but generally, the lowest pricing tier aimed to capture about 80% of residential households.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The second tier had 15% of households while the third highest tier covered the remaining 5%.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Hong Kong has two major suppliers of household electricity, namely HK Electric and China Light and Power.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Both of them offer tiered pricing, with as many as seven tiers.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: According to the Hong Kong Environment and Ecology Bureau, tiered pricing is deployed for residential consumers to "promote energy efficiency and conservation".

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Tiered tariffs can also be found in a host of other jurisdictions, including the United States (US), the United Kingdom (UK) and South Africa.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: In fact, a World Bank study of 60 developed and developing countries showed that 60% of countries surveyed made use of tiered pricing or volumetric IBTs.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The study noted that the rationale for a tiered pricing structure was to provide a "social safety net" whereby all consumers could assess a basic subsistence volume of consumption at a very affordable tariff, while ensuring that the revenue shortfall was covered by surcharges on the largest consumers.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The study found that volumetric IBTs had "a material effect on affordability".

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: MTI stated that electricity should be priced at its "full cost of production and delivery" and warned of "inadvertent implications".

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The Minister gave an example of a multi-generational household paying more if they lived in a single home, than in two smaller homes.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: While this may be true, this phenomenon already exists in many Government policies.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The larger, multi-generational household is already receiving less Service and Conservancy Charges (S&CC) and U-Save rebates, has less subsidies for long-term care, may be disqualified from the Silver Support Scheme and so on.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: There is probably no policy with perfect outcomes.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: So, let us not let perfect be enemy of the good.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: This could be done by charging lower rates at non-peak hours.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The EMA is already doing this for business consumers.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Business consumers can make use of EMA's Demand Side Management (DSM) scheme to lower their electricity bills, by adjusting when and how much electricity they use.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Businesses can participate in the Demand Response programme, where they can voluntarily reduce electricity usage when prices are high.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Such behaviour also benefits the system, as it reduces the capacity required at peak periods.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: It is well-known that a key driver of the costs of producing electricity is not the total load, but the peak hour load.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Having a cheaper rate for off-peak consumption would benefit the system as a whole, as it will go towards ensuring that the peak demand can be more efficiently met by the existing transmission grid.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Can such differentiated peak and non-peak pricing be applied to households as well?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Such time of use charging has been offered for decades around the world, in major cities including London, San Francisco and Sydney.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Under this pilot programme, Singaporean households will be issued with smart meters and will receive alerts to actively reduce consumption during peak hours, in exchange for financial reward, such as rebates.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: This scheme is, in effect, a differential pricing scheme based on time of use.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The Government's planned financial incentives to reduce peak hour consumption could be further developed.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: We could work towards a system where the electricity tariff for off-peak consumption for households is lower than the tariff for peak hour consumption.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: This allows households to manage their electricity costs by adjusting their time of use.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Nonetheless, with the concerns about global energy supply and costs looming in the horizon, this is an issue that deserves attention.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Such reforms would recognise that electricity is a basic good and yet, incentivise energy conservation.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It is especially apt to describe the ongoing inflationary pressures faced by Singaporeans as a crisis.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Since the COVID-19 pandemic, when many Singaporeans are still struggling financially, the cost of almost everything in Singapore has gone up.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In contrast, the Government does not seem to be too concerned about this crisis and continues to add oil to the fire.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Food prices have surged because NTUC FairPrice stood by instead of doing more.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I still remember, in the early 1970s, I used to queue up at a community centre with my mother to buy heavily-discounted basic foodstuff and necessities supplied by NTUC.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Today, NTUC FairPrice's prices are not even the lowest in the market.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It is commonly known that lower prices can be found at the Sheng Siong supermarket instead.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It appears that the role of NTUC and, by implication, that of the Government, has changed drastically over the last few decades.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: NTUC FairPrice no longer serves as the anchor of price stability.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The Government, instead of being the independent referee and price stabiliser in the economy, has become a profit-seeker in direct competition with the private sector.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In many sectors, the Government is the market maker and has influenced the price levels in those sectors, the most obvious and problematic one being the property market.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Hence, the current cost of living crisis faced by Singaporeans is not entirely due to the global supply chain disruption arising from the COVID-19 pandemic and the war in Ukraine.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The COVID-19 pandemic has exposed the fact that Singaporeans have little savings to weather financial emergencies.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The events after the pandemic have only exacerbated the situation that Singaporeans have been subject to by the Government over the recent decades.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Singaporeans have been worried about the cost of living for many years because they feel that their wages have not kept up with the cost of goods and services that they need to lead a meaningful life in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: CDC vouchers, GST vouchers, Service and Conservancy Charges (S&CC) rebates and so on can be very helpful for Singaporeans in the short term, but these handouts do not solve the fundamental structural issues that are at the heart of the rising cost of living in Singapore today.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: To help Singaporeans get out of this cost of living crisis, the PSP believes that we will need to nudge the Government to change its two favourite financial management approaches, namely, the "pay and pay" and "the chicken wing for a whole chicken" approaches.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The Government's approaches may have served us well in the early days of nation-building when public finances were tight and wages rising fast.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: However, they may not be appropriate in today's context when wages are not rising as fast as the cost of living.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It is especially worrying if more and more middle-class Singaporeans cannot keep up with the current standard of living.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: First, let us talk about "pay and pay".

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Many Singaporeans often jokingly refer to the People's Action Party (PAP) as a "pay and pay" party because it seems to run Singapore like a company and operates like a profit-seeker.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: PSP has spoken many times in this House that this Government has ample fiscal resources and, yet, it has always tried to justify increasing taxes and fees for public services whenever possible.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: PSP has objected many times to the increase in the GST from 7% to 9%.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: While we agree that public services like electricity, water, public transport and so on should be operated efficiently, the ultimate objective should be to maximise long-term social benefits and not short-term profits.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The Government should price public services based on long-term considerations to provide stability to Singaporeans' livelihoods, which will increase long-term social benefits.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Our fiscal resources have been hoarded away in the Reserves, supposedly for the sake of the future generation.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: But this is to the detriment of the present generation who are facing the heavy and unnecessary burden of higher taxation and rising cost of living.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We urgently need to review how our fiscal resources, including our Reserves, are being used before we contemplate raising taxes on the people.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The Reserves and Budget should serve Singaporeans and not the other way around.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: More discerning Singaporeans have pointed out long ago that the PAP Government likes to give Singaporeans a chicken wing and then take back a whole chicken.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Essentially, what it means is that the Government is a shrewd financial manager who gives out occasional short-term handouts but commits Singaporeans to long-term payment schemes that require them to pay out consistently over the long term.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The total long-term payouts will be much larger than the short-term handouts.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: For every Build-To-Order (BTO) flat sold, the buyer will have to pay hundreds of thousands for the land cost and have to take up a housing loan to service it.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In exchange, the Government will sweeten the deal by giving out CPF Housing Grants of $30,000 to $60,000 through HDB.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It begs the question why can the Government not waive the land cost so that Singaporeans can keep the half a million dollars in their CPF account for retirement instead?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This is exactly what the PSP has proposed in the affordable home scheme, which waives land cost for owner occupiers of HDB flats.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It is obvious that, in this way, Singaporeans' financial position will be significantly improved and that will yield a lot of social benefits.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: For MediShield and CareShield, the Government has also been accumulating large surpluses ahead of actual expenditures.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: If premiums can be reduced, Singaporeans will have more balances in their MediSave Accounts to earn more interest while they are young.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: PSP has proposed for the Government to pay for the MediShield and CareShield premiums all together and establish a universal health scheme for Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It is not an overstatement to say that "a chicken wing for a whole chicken" approach is the main cause of social anxiety for Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: He said that Singaporeans still want a good material life, but the Singapore dream is also about finding fulfilment, meaning and purpose.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: PSP wholeheartedly agrees that there is more to life than material success and consumption.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I have also spoken about self-fulfillment and ikigai, which is "purpose" in Japanese, in the public.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: But we believe that Singaporeans are no longer talking so much about the 5Cs because the structural issues in our economy and the cost of living crisis have now made the 5Cs completely unattainable for many middle-class Singaporeans even if they are frugal and work hard.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Today, condominiums and cars are unaffordable on a middle-class salary.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Even motorcycles feel out of reach for many Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It is well-known that country club membership fees have soared because of the influx of wealthy foreigners.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Of the 5Cs, the credit card is the most attainable, but the credit card has fallen into a necessity to facilitate "buy now, pay later" when cash is tight.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Singaporeans are talking less about the 5Cs not because they do not want it anymore but because for many Singaporeans today, it really can only be a dream.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: An urgent reset of our policies is needed to address the structural issues that our economy faces.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Singaporeans must have more to look forward to than the rising cost of living.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Economic growth must lead to rising real incomes and better lives for everyone and not just a select few.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We must help Singaporeans to improve their long-term financial well-being so that they will have the savings to withstand emergencies like the COVID-19 pandemic.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The financial leeway will also allow Singaporeans to have the freedom to develop their potential, which will be beneficial to our economy in the long term.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Over the last three years, my primary focus in this House is to speak on policies to improve the financial well-being of Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Today, I will put all these into an integrated cost of living relief package with the following five measures.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: One, first and foremost, reduce GST to 7% to clearly demonstrate the Government's determination to dampen the inflationary psychology.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This will also be a much-needed spending boost for the nascent post-COVID-19 recovery; Three, introduce the affordable home scheme and Millennial Apartments scheme to make HDB flats more affordable, strengthen retirement adequacy and offer more choices to young Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Four, introduce a universal health scheme for Singaporeans, essentially based on the Government-paid MediShield and CareShield premiums for Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: PSP has also estimated that it is manageable with the fiscal resources we have currently.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We hope the Government will make improving the financial well-being of Singaporeans the cornerstone of our new social compact.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: I recognise that Singaporeans are going through this, but we have to recognise that this is a global phenomenon and we have to tackle this together.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: But, Sir, I have been listening carefully and intently to the speeches made by the three Opposition Members of Parliament and my impression is that they are basically asking for an ultimate reduction in tariffs, some reduction in taxes, more top-ups, more handouts.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: It did not surprise me that Mr Leong Mun Wai, again, talked about the GST.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: Honestly, Mr Speaker, Sir, I think the Opposition Members of Parliament have been milking the GST cow for a very long time and we have explained time and again over the last several years why the GST increase is necessary and why there are offset packages.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: So, maybe I just want to say if you really must milk something, go and milk another cow.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: But at the back of my mind, I would like to ask the Opposition Members of Parliament if one day you are to steer this ship – I hope not, but we cannot rule it out completely – if you are to steer this ship, what is your overall underlying strategy?

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: Because, so far, what I have heard is that you are basically dissecting the problem and you are talking about water, electricity, GST, so on and so forth.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: But at the end of the day, we need to balance the Budget and we need to balance the Budget for all Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: Do you know what is more sorrowful than feeling sorrowful and despair?

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: It is when it becomes hopeless; it is when we no longer have a chance.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: But, clearly, this is not the situation we are in.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: So, I think it is important that all of us in this Chamber – PAP Members of Parliament, Opposition Members of Parliament, WP Members of Parliament, PSP Members of Parliament, Nominated Members of Parliament (NMPs) and Non-Constituency Members of Parliament (NCMPs) – come together and let us tackle this problem collectively.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: I noticed that the WP's Motion used the word "crisis", cost of living crisis.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: I shiver and shudder for a while when I saw the word "crisis" because crisis means, I think somebody is going to suggest a draw on Reserves.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: I would not classify it as a crisis.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: We have not lost hope because we have a lot of opportunities.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: Discuss this issue of cost of living by asking three honest questions and, hopefully, by giving three honest answers also.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: The first question: is there pain amongst Singaporeans due to the rising cost of living due to inflation?

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: And the answer is yes, there is pain.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: We have to acknowledge it and we have to admit this is going to be a rough and bumpy ride for all of us.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: But, sometimes, as we overcome difficulties, there are also learning points and I am completely certain in my mind that we will overcome this.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: The worst may not have come yet, the worst may well come later.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: Let us help those who need the most help and not only help them the most but maybe help them for the longest time possible.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: It is an unequal policy, but I think it is the right policy to adopt.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: Clearly, the answer is no. ﻿As I have said, we will target assistance and help to those who need it more and hopefully for a longer period, and we will do the right thing.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: And doing the right thing is not about just policies or rules and regulations.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: We all know that doing the right thing is what is in your heart.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: And doing the right thing is – I hope the Opposition Members of Parliament will agree me – definitely not about straddling the middle ground to gain some votes.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: We will never do that and we do not want to start doing that.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: So, I say, let us all behave like a herd.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: We are the Singapore Herd because, united we are strong and divided we become weak.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: And, Sir, here I would like to admit and also acknowledge that most of us, it is human nature, we like consistency and continuity.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: Many of us do not like change, especially when change involves an increase in the cost of living, it involves inflation.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: But I think it is something we have to accept collectively.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: It is a global phenomenon and we will overcome this.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: Every generation has to solve their own problems and down the road.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: And just now, the hon Member Mr Leong Mun Wai talked about Reserves again.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: I just want to say this: actually, in reality, neither him nor me are qualified to talk about our Reserves.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: We are only the custodians, and you know what?

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: But I think if every time we come across a problem and a difficulty, we ask for the key to the safe and we start taking out, there is not going to be very much left in the safe, you know.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: I am always very marvelled by this mahjong table because on every mahjong table, there are four players and there is always a drawer there for each player.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: Every time I look at it – and some people put their chips on the table and some put theirs inside the drawer – my reading of it is that what is on the table are MAS and Temasek.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: During the Asian Financial Crisis, we all know that the currencies around us were all hammered, beaten down.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: We got off relatively unscathed and do you really think that the hedge funds did not look at us?

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: But I think they probably say, "You know, this little island, I do not know how much is inside that drawer, I better not mess with them because it is like throwing a boomerang.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: You throw a boomerang, hoping to hit the other guy, it comes back and it slit your throat." So, let us safeguard our Reserves and unless it is a real crisis like COVID-19, I think try not to touch it.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: Mr Leong Mun Wai will understand this because he is Cantonese.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: When the cow goes to the river and drinks, if it does not want to drink, you cannot press its head down.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: So, Mr Speaker, Sir, my point is that as long as we stay united, cohesive, we will overcome this.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: We must have the guts, the gumption and the resolve to do this correctly.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: And rather than seek out the heat, we should look for the light and I am very confident that we will overcome this.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: The more vulnerable, those who need help will get it more and get it longer.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: And basically, this quote shows how important it is that we stay united as one people.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: And I quote Mr Lee Kuan Yew, "For the next thousand years, we will still be here, recognisable, identifiable."

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: So, it will be wrong of him to say that I am asking for more subsidies from the Government or raiding whatever fund to do that.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: The second proposal which I suggested was about time of use pricing.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: And I also mentioned that MTI is already in the process of giving financial incentives to households who consume electricity at off-peak hours and they are also doing that with business consumers already.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: Can I, through you, confirm with Member Sitoh Yih Pin that I did not recommend a drawdown of the reserves?

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin
text: And when I hear you say that, I began to shiver and shudder.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: However, in the last half a year, the frequency of such feedback has really increased tremendously.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: I receive such feedback not merely from residents who are in the lower-income brackets.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: I also receive feedback from across the different income tiers.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Recently, I attended a feedback session with some condominium residents in Hougang and concerns arising on rising costs of living were raised by many with whom I spoke to.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: I therefore support the WP's Motion today calling on the Government to review its policy with a view to lower cost of living pressures on Singaporeans and their families.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: There are different issues of rising costs of living which affects Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: My colleagues in the WP will be focusing on different aspects on the rising cost pressures.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: I will be speaking on the need to relook some aspects of our means testing criteria in public healthcare and for more help for adults with special needs or disabilities and their caregiving families.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: The current economic indicators applied to the healthcare means testing criteria may have their limitations.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: One, the formula looks at the rigid household incomes and does not look at deferring or specific needs of specific members of each household when evaluating help which should be given.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: While it is true that both the young, such as children and the elderly, may not have earning power or contribute directly to the PCHI, the elderly are more likely to require nursing care due to the onset of various chronic illnesses associated with ageing.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Approximately 75% of those aged 70 to 74 years had hypertension and 60% in the same age group had high cholesterol.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: These chronic illnesses often result in increased healthcare spending, including expenses related to complications.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: For example, diabetes and high cholesterol are commonly associated with cardiovascular diseases, like coronary heart diseases.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: In fact, in 2019, approximately 75% of heart attack patients were aged 60 and above.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Furthermore, most corporate medical insurance plans typically allow employees to include two family dependents, usually a spouse and offspring but do not permit the inclusion of elderly dependents.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: This exclusion is often reflected in corporate insurance plans, such as those by Raffles Medical Group, a major corporate insurance provider in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: These plans specify that eligible dependents must be either a spouse or unmarried or unemployed children.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: It is crucial that we consider such disparities in means testing.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: One may argue that the seniors in Singapore already have access to a wide range of subsidy schemes aimed at addressing their needs, such as the Merdeka Generation Package (MGP) and the Pioneer Generation Package (PGP).

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: However, a closer examination of these subsidies offered by these packages reveals room for improvement.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: For instance, the subsidies entitlement for MG and PG cardholders cover chronic conditions and dental services, but not as extensive in coverage when compared with the coverage of critical illnesses in commonly available medical insurance policies and subsidies for chronic conditions are kept annually.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Two, it does not look at whether a family member actually do receive help from family members for their medical fees and expenses of a family member.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: The choice of residence for retired elderly individuals, whether they decide to stay with their working adult children or live independently, has little impact on the family's financial dynamics.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Financial support from working adult children is a personal decision arrived independently of the elderly person's choice of living arrangement.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: While the Government expects family members to pay for the living and medical expenses of family members, in reality, this may be easier said than done.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Many residents have told me that they do not wish to impose on their children and they try to make do with what they have.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Many have tried unsuccessfully to get public financial assistance when they do not receive sufficient money from their children, as their children have told them they do not have enough to contribute to their parents, including those who live with their children in the same households.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: How can such people receive further subsidy or assistance if help is not forthcoming from family members, without having to request from family members?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: I see the same problem with some of my residents seeking financial assistance but were not eligible because of a household income.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: An elderly male resident saw me a few times, crying with frustration, due to the lack of financial support as he is not eligible for more support, due to his son's and daughter-in-law's incomes and his son said that he is unable to provide more support.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Furthermore, for healthcare means testing, beyond cases of elderly parents living with working children, there may also be other categories of core occupiers in the same household who may not be currently sharing or co-funding medical expenses of other occupiers of the property.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: By way of an example, Mr A is in his early 60s and working part-time due to his health condition.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: They share common household expenses, but not individual medical expenses.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: The household income will be a key consideration for the amount of subsidy he is entitled under the current PCHI formula.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: In a case like this, does the Government expect Mr A to reach out to his siblings to ask them to share his medical expenses?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Will Mr A get help, maybe applies to the authorities for further subsidy?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: In July this year, the hon Member for Aljunied GRC Mr Gerald Giam, urged MOH to consider removing the AV component for household so with no income.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Senior Parliamentary Secretary Ms Rahayu Mahzam said in response and I quote, "On the Member's point of considering to remove this, this is a broader point we are looking at." I hope the Government will consider removing this.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: The Minister for Health himself has acknowledged in a written answer to a PQ in February this year that AV is an imperfect proxy for determining financial need, especially for those who are asset-rich but cash-poor.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: There may be a variety of reasons why such individual owners are unable to monetise their property.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: As we age, we may grow more attached to our homes, the neighbourhoods we are familiar with and the communities we have built over the years and that this may not even be the reasons for some, amongst us, for not being able to move out to a lower priced property.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: For whatever reasons, monetising, right-sizing or downsizing may not always be feasible or desirable.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: In addition, we have been encouraged to age-in-place.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: But owners living in their own properties are not the only people who are affected by the AV issue.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: There are also family members who are caught by the rule.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Besides non-owner spouses, there are siblings, children, aunts, uncles and cousins who may be living in the same property who may be caught by this rule.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Such family members may not be able to get their relatives in the same household to pay for their medical expenses.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: They may not be able to afford a place of their own just to qualify or more state subsidies.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: There are also cases of family members being co-owners of a family property or co-inheriting such property after a parent has passed on.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: I know a few of such cases where residents inherited a family property together with fellow family members.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: They continue to live in their own property.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Family properties is kept for use by other family members and this could be a residential or even commercial property.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: And there is no near-term prospect of the property being sold and proceeds to be distributed.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: These non-occupier owners are caught by the AV issue when it comes to medical subsidies and also for other packages and schemes from other Ministries.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Such people have to appeal every time against their non-access for subsidies or benefits and an outcome may not always be consistent.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Before I leave this point, I would also say that whether a person is an owner or non-owner, it would not be right to expect a person living in a property with higher AV battling a serious disease to have to make arrangements to move out of his or her home or to sell his or her home to raise funds for the very medical treatment he or she needs.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Next, Mr Speaker, I would like to discuss the needs of families who have family members with special needs or with mental health issues and requiring care for family members.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: The burden placed upon these families is immense and I hope that the state can extend more help.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: While the numbers of such families may not be large, their plight is significant and warrants our attention.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: These numbers are not negligible and we must recognise the challenges faced by these families.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: These figures underscore the urgency of addressing their needs.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Moreover, for families where such adults with special needs or mental issues require their ageing parents to continue to care for them, the burden of caregiving, both physically and financially, can be tremendous.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: I have some suggestions to provide for better assistance to these families.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: One, we should create a list of non-critical illnesses that necessitate long-term care and force individuals out of employment.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: This list would include conditions, such as early onset dementia, severe autism, Down Syndrome, schizophrenia and Parkinson's disease.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Such conditions can be financially burdensome for families and access to social support for these individuals and their families is currently limited.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Many insurance plans cover critical illnesses and the insurance products available on the market that cover non-critical illnesses remain limited.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Besides, some of these non-critical illnesses are congenital, making afflicted individuals excluded from medical insurance scheme, which require that one must be free of pre-existing medical conditions before they are onboarded.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: The eligibility criteria of CareShield Life can be expanded to include consideration of those who can still perform ADLs but are unable to earn a stable income due to non-critical illnesses.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: This aligns with the original intentions of CareShield Life, which is targeted at individuals with long-term care needs.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Two, for such individuals with non-critical illnesses, we should offer more subsidies with medical supplies, consultations, treatment, rehabilitation and daycare services.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Medical expenses of such injuries are not limited to specialist outpatient care or inpatient care, but also included other essential areas like medical supplies and rehabilitation.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Three, increase subsidies for inpatient and outpatient specialist treatment for both individuals with non-critical illnesses and their caregivers should be made available.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: While there are existing subsidies for long-term residential care, daycare and rehabilitation, many families do not meet the eligibility criteria due to the ceiling limit set by the PCHI or even the annual value of their property.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: This can make it challenging for working adults taking care of their disabled children as their income may exceed this limit.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: The family only marginally qualifies for 30% subsidies and entitlement for daycare services.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Furthermore, the Senior Mobility Fund is targeted as seniors aged 60 and above, leaving out younger persons with disabilities (PwDs) who also require nursing and rehabilitation support.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: In short, I am concerned that those affected are not getting enough support.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: There are PwDs in the working age group with rehabilitation needs and I hope the Senior Mobility Fund is extended to include these.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: I also hope that PwDs in the working adult age groups qualify for subtleties in daycare and residential care.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Beside the opportunity cost of loss income, they should not be penalised just because they live with a working family member out of necessity.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Four, more support should be given to caregivers of adults with special needs or disabilities.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: While we do have existing grants and concessions, such as the Caregivers Training Grant, Home Caregiving Grant and Migrant Domestic Levy Concession, some of these are limited to households where the care recipient is elderly and exclude families where elderly parents are caregivers to disabled children.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Can caregiving grants such as the Home Caregiving Grant and the Migrant Domestic Levy Concession for aged persons with disabilities be extended the household where the care recipients are not seniors and may have no ADL issues but are involuntarily unemployed because of their medical condition.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: After all, the conditions that threaten employment, for example, early onset dementia, severe autism, Down Syndrome, schizophrenia and so on, are neurological or psychiatric conditions that affect soft skills, like cognitive and communication skills, and may not always affect one's ability to perform ADLs.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: And so, to use ADLs as an indicator and an eligibility determination for the grant is not comprehensive.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: In closing, Mr Speaker, I hope the current means testing formula can be further improved upon to take into account the specifics of an individual's financial situation, particularly his or her cash flow and health condition, and make healthcare more affordable and accessible for all.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: More help should be extended to adults with special needs or other forms of disabilities who are in the working adult age group but are unable to work and requires part or full-time care from family members, especially families where the parents are getting on in age.

speaker: Mr Speaker
