text: I suspend the Sitting and will take the Chair at 4.25 pm.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Sitting accordingly suspended  at 4.05 pm until 4.25 pm.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Announcements of price increases in transport fares, water and utilities came one after another.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: COE prices rose to record highs and GST is going to be increased by another 1% next year.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: All these are adding on to the anxieties of Singaporeans over the ever-rising cost of living that seems endless.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: These anxieties cannot be alleviated by the various aid packages that the Government has rolled out, because while the packages are for a limited time, the cost increases are here to stay.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The growing sense of insecurity, or even depression for some, over their declining ability to meet expenses or maintain previous lifestyles on their own income, can never be addressed with Government handouts.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The rising cost in Singapore is not only affecting the people, but businesses too.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Whilst our low corporate tax was able to compensate for our high-cost space and attracting foreign investments, this tool would no longer be available with the implementation of Base Erosion and Profit Shifting (BEPS) 2.0, which sets a minimum corporate tax rate.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This adds on to the urgency to find ways of containing costs in Singapore.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: One of our major cost component is cost of property.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: For most of us, buying a home is the single largest expenditure of our lifetime.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Hence, high residential property price has a huge impact on our cost of living.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In the retail sector, rental accounts for about 30% of the business cost.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: So, for each item that we buy from a shop, about 30% of their costs goes towards paying for the rental of the shop.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Prices has been rising in food outlets, like coffee shops and food courts.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Hawkers spoke of alarming increases in rents imposed by the landlords.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Record prices in the transaction of such properties are caused for concern.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In 2022, following the announcement of the GST hike, the Committee Against Profiteering (CAP) was reconvened to investigate feedback on unjustified price increases of products and services.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I was invited by the Leader of the Opposition to be the representative of the Opposition on the Committee and having attended two meetings, I have learnt how limited the scope is for this Committee to act against profiteering.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The Committee acts on complaints received from members of the public.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Such complaints are mostly against retailers, especially hawkers.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: At the retail level, there is much competition.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: So, I am not surprised that investigation usually reviewed that there are other reasons for the price increase.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: For example, the increase in price might be due to higher rents.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I raise this point at our last meeting and suggested the secretariat look further up the supply chain.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I look forward to hearing from MTI on the progress at our next meeting.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Price Kaki, an app that compares retail prices from different sellers and seeks to prevent profiteering is also only able to check on vendors at the retail level.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Places like Ireland, California, Canada, Scotland, Spain and China impose a cap on the rent increase each year.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Austria and Germany are planning to do so as well.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The intention is not to depress prices to low levels, but to curb excesses.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This can serve to stabilise the property market and pre-empt excessive rent increase.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In addition, real estate agents are commonly paid a commission based on the rent and, hence, higher rents work to their benefit.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It would, therefore, benefit tenants to have an alternative source of information on what constitutes a reasonable rent increase.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Record COE prices for private and commercial vehicles, and even motorcycles, are causing pain for both families and businesses.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We understand the need to control the vehicle population in Singapore, because we are a small nation and road space is limited, but we must also recognise that mobility and the benefits that it provides are essential for all and should not be the sole province of the rich.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Skyrocketing COE prices contribute to the cost of living crisis in many ways.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: If the cost of a motorcycle doubles because the price of the COE has tripled, the Grab delivery rider is going to have to be paid more for his work.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The Senior Minister of State for Transport said yesterday that this would not change things much as there are not many households with multiple cars.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Can the Senior Minister of State show us the comparison of the number of households with multiple cars versus those with multiple properties, to explain the difference in approach?

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In any case, imposing levies on second and subsequent cars would either dampen demand for multiple cars and tilt the balance in favour of those buying their first cars, or else raise additional revenue for Government.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The most likely outcome is a combination of both.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: As both outcomes are desirable, I see no reason to reject this suggestion.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Another way to cope with rising cost of living is to have higher wages.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Today, I will focus on the training and education for higher-paying jobs.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The wage gap between graduates and non-graduates has been widening significantly, suggesting that there is demand for more graduates and we should provide more university places for our students.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Why do we not increase medical intake more aggressively?

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Instead, our students end up going to overseas medical schools, incurring huge expenses and we risk unnecessary brain drain when they do not return.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The traditional argument about ensuring fair share of talents in various sectors is outdated when we import foreign talents so readily.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The same applies to other faculties as well, where Singaporean students are keen to study and that would lead to good paying jobs.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Many suggestions have been, and will be, made today to address this pressing issue and improve the lives of Singaporeans.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I hope the Government can keep an open mind to all suggestions and consider them seriously.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I think this offers a good reason to review our approach towards our Reserves and how much more do we need to accumulate.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: If our TFR falls further from cost pressures, who are we accumulating the Reserves for?

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: We must, and we should, take these concerns seriously, and it is our solemn duty to approach these concerns with the seriousness it deserves.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: It affects the daily lives of our people, the vitality of our markets and the health of our national economy.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: As I hear the debates from some of the Members on the floor, like Mr Sitoh, it invokes in me images of insurmountable challenges and despair.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: We must, therefore, use this term judiciously, especially when the resolve of a nation like ours is called into question.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: I stand today, not to minimise the concerns of our citizens regarding the cost of living, but to contextualise the narrative we choose to represent it.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: It is our collective responsibility to analyse and approach this issue with a clear-eyed perspective, and not through the lens of panic that the word "crisis" might imply.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: That our systems are in disarray and that our societal frameworks are on the brink of failure.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: Singapore stands today as a global hub of commerce, a testament to sound economic principles and a beacon of stability.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: This did not happen by chance, but through the meticulous crafting of policies that are both robust and responsive.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: Today, we stand united in our commitment to tackle a concern that lies at the core of every Singaporean's daily life – the escalating cost of living.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: But these are not just random fluctuations; they are the result of complex global economic trends, including widespread inflation that many countries are dealing with.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: While we see a moderate level of inflation as a hallmark of a thriving economy, the excess erodes the economic well-being of both companies and consumers.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: The businesses that drive our economy are feeling the effects of today's unpredictable economic climate first-hand.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: We have seen the cost of running a business go up due to higher prices for materials and goods, a consequence of the pandemic's lingering disruption to how we get products from one place to another.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: Additionally, recent international tensions have caused prices for fuel and food to soar – expenses that not only affected companies, but also the daily budgets of every household.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: The price of rice, for example, a staple in every Singaporean home, has been subjected to fluctuations due to trade restrictions and weather-related production issues in exporting countries.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: These challenges are complex, but they have very real impacts on our community, from the corner store to the dinner table.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: It is imperative to acknowledge that the weight of these escalating costs cannot be shouldered by the business community alone.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: With each incremental rise in operating expenses, there is a cascade of effects, impacting on employment, wages and the price of goods and services.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: Mr Liang Eng Hwa has already mentioned that our Government has not been a passive observer to these trends.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: Through monetary policy, they have taken decisive steps, countering the cost of imports by allowing the Singapore dollar to appreciate in a controlled manner.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: This is a strategic move, managing the immediate needs with medium-term outcomes, and is but one prong of their approach.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: On the fiscal front, the Government have been responsive.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: Consider the Assurance Package enhancements announced in Budget 2023, which introduced or expanded upon several initiatives; the Cost of Living Special Payment provides a direct relief to families, helping to mitigate the immediate impact of rising prices; U-Save rebates have been a buffer for households against the increasing utility bills as energy prices soared globally.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: These measures are carefully designed to ensure that the additional costs are not borne by those least able to shoulder them.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: The Enterprise Innovation Scheme (EIS) and the enhancements to the SME Co-Investment Fund exemplify the commitment to fostering a fertile environment for businesses to innovate and grow.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: A concrete manifestation of this commitment is seen in our investment in the tech industry, supporting the creation of high-value jobs and the development of cutting-edge products that not only serve local needs but have the potential to meet demands internationally.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: As we continue to bolster our economic resilience, we must also fortify the social fabric that holds us together.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: This involves maintaining fiscal responsibility and optimising social support measures to effectively reach those hardest hit by cost of living adjustments.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: A clear example is the enhancements made to the Child Development Account (CDA), providing additional support to young families investing in their children's future.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: Alongside these measures, the Government has been monitoring the business sector to safeguard against any instances of profiteering, which many consumers are concerned about.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: Even as global inflationary measures are set to moderate going forward, Singapore must continue to navigate cost of living issues in a way that is responsible, effective and forward-looking.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: The business community urges all stakeholders in society – individuals, families, community leaders, businesses, investors and the Government, to work together in trusted partnership towards a sustainable and viable growth that all of us, as a national collective, will benefit meaningfully from.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: As we look ahead, the business community call for four key shared commitments.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: Our first shared commitment is to understand the root causes of our cost of living challenges with clarity and precision.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: We are not just facing local issues, nor can it be solely attributed to ineffective policy-making.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: We are dealing with the ripple effects of global market trends and geopolitical events that have affected many countries, including Singapore.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: We therefore need to dissect these complex dynamics thoroughly.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: By doing so, we can craft solutions that are right for our unique situation in Singapore while also fitting into the larger global puzzle.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: A common pitfall for many nations has been the reliance on policy-making grounded in evidence or statistics that unfortunately are reflective of past conditions rather than the present reality.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: Such a lag can lead to suboptimal outcomes.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: Take, for instance, the Federal Reserve, which, having underestimated inflationary trends, found itself compelled to implement rapid interest rate hikes.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: To refine our policy-making, a more dynamic approach is called for.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: This could be achieved through enhanced collaboration with trade associations, ensuring a continuous dialogue and close listening ear between their diverse membership and Government policy-makers.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: Such a two-way exchange promises to bring real-time ground-level insights to the forefront, allowing for the crafting of more responsive and agile solutions to the economic challenges we face and allow policy-makers at times to consider slowing down the pace of implementation of certain policies that could unintentionally aggravate inflation woes.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: Our second commitment is to uphold strict fiscal discipline to protect our economic future.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: It is essential that we sharpen the focus of our social support programmes, ensuring they deliver tangible outcomes to those most affected by rising costs.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: We must continue to reward innovation and productivity across all sectors.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: By doing so, we are not just spending money more wisely but also strengthening the foundation of our economic system.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: The third cornerstone of our approach is a commitment to thoughtful policy-making, avoiding quick fixes that cause more problems than they solve.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: Our aim is to create a cycle of prosperity, spurring growth that leads to better wages and smoothing out inefficiencies that inflate costs.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: Our fourth commitment is fortifying the bonds of our community.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: In a landscape where the cost of living is escalating, it is not only households that feel the strain.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: The repercussions extend deeply into the business community as well.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: Workers naturally seek higher wages from their employers to cope with their increasing expenses.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: These initiatives demonstrate a clear national resolve to uplift the standards of living for this vulnerable group.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: From a business perspective, these measures might initially seem like an added strain on operational costs.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: Yet, the broader business community understands that these are the tenets of a new social compact that Singapore is striving to create.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: In our journey to overcome and adjust to the evolving challenges of cost of living, it calls for unity and collective resolve, not division.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: We must resist the inclination to frame our challenges as conflicts between different segments of our society, be it local versus foreigner, business versus worker, or Government versus citizen.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: Instead, we must recognise that these economic hurdles are shared challenges that will be best overcome when we, as a united nation, pull together in the same direction.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: Fostering this unity requires a commitment from all sectors of society to engage in open, constructive dialogue.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: We must break down the barriers that hinder collaboration and build bridges that allow us to share insights and develop holistic solutions.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: By standing in solidarity – citizens and Government, businesses and workers, locals and internationals – we can harness the full strength of our national character to address the cost of living issues in a manner that is not only effective but also equitable.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: While we acknowledge the language of "crisis" may capture the immediacy of the issue, we must frame our dialogue in a manner that reflects not panic but preparedness, not reaction but readiness.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: But even when we may be faced with "crisis fatigue", what affects us viscerally is the surging prices of things that we need on a daily basis.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: (In Mandarin):   In recent years, many things have troubled Singaporeans, especially the pressure of rising living costs.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: This also includes rising medical and nursing costs.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Among these, mental health is also an aspect that may be easy to neglect in Singapore's medical and insurance systems as it is less visible.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: However, mental health can have a very direct impact on the lives of individuals and their families.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: We must remember that if we neglect our physical and mental health for a while, we may need more complex or even expensive treatment later on and the stress we need to endure in life will also increase.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Some may point out that this is a waste of resources, that it will reduce personal savings that can be used for medical care in the future, and also creates dependence on the country and weakens the country's financial resources in the long run.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: The Workers' Party believes health cannot be understood through a cost lens alone.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Health is a long-term investment in our people and the country.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Preventive care or regular care today can effectively avoid future health and financial burdens.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: I will use my speech on the motion today to explore these issues in more depth, with the hope of improving medical services and reducing the challenges faced by Singaporeans.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: (In English): The adverse impact of the cost of living crisis is seen on both mental and physical health.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: While humans have an immense capacity for resilience to get through difficult times, there are measurable, long-term effects on health and overall wellbeing that result from long-term stress.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: The imbalance in the body's physiology due to long-term stress, such as the constant worries associated with increasing costs, can lead to increased rates of chronic illnesses such as cardiovascular disease, lowered immunity, leading to greater susceptibility to infectious diseases, and also has an adverse impact on mental health.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: I would therefore like to focus on the health and care related elements of the cost of living crisis facing us.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: There is attention given to the direct link between worries over costs and the impact that it is having our ability to stay healthy and to be able to afford care, be it physical or mental health, long-term intermediate care or even preventive care.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: A report released by Cigna in January 2023 about a global survey of 9,000 respondents also warned that cost of living pressures could trigger a global health crisis.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: The survey found that rising costs of living are top of mind for most people around the globe, with nearly half of respondents in Singapore saying that it was their biggest worry.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Almost two thirds of the 1,100 respondents in Singapore also agreed that inflation is making it too expensive to stay healthy, whether it is through paying for care or taking measures to stay healthy.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: A study at King's College London's Centre for Society and Mental Health also found that worries about increasing costs pose a major risk to mental health and those with pre-existing mental health issues are more at risk.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: The study also found that those who are using savings to meet everyday costs and borrowing money to cope were correlated to psychological distress.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: In view of this, I believe the cost of health and other forms of care is one of the areas that warrants closer attention as we tackle the broader cost of living issues.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: The health outcomes we have achieved at this cost are rightly a point of pride for policy-makers.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: However, our country is a densely populated urban city where the cost of healthcare delivery is more easily managed compared with countries with larger and sparser geographies.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Singapore's health system also benefits from a generally lower crime and drug abuse rate and road traffic fatality rate than other countries – achievements that are not to be diminished and these should definitely be maintained.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: But I believe that our health outcomes could be improved, with Singaporeans living healthier, longer and safer lives.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: In terms of waiting times, medical manpower per capita, intensive care unit (ICU) bed capacity in the public health system, there remains concerns about what the tensions in these areas mean for our health outcomes.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: These areas should bear continuous scrutiny to maintain confidence in our public healthcare system.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Out of pocket costs and waiting times are the most direct interaction that most of us would have with the healthcare system.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: This is indicative of residents being extremely cognisant about the potential costs associated with ill health and wanting to take action to guard against these costs.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: A Straits Times article published in April 2022 titled "Having an Integrated Shield Plan and rider may not always guarantee peace of mind" warned that even buying IPs and riders may not always guarantee peace of mind and that residents might still face substantial bills should they require expensive treatment for preexisting conditions.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Recent commentary has also focused on private insurance coverage for those with mental health conditions and there is acknowledgement that current coverage is inadequate.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: In a reply to a question that I filed in September this year, MOH also stated that insurers cannot indiscriminately reject an application solely on, amongst others, the basis of medical conditions, including mental health conditions.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: I was also happy to see an article in end October 2023 where private insurers stated that they are looking to include better coverage for those with mental healthcare and treatment needs.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: However, the Government should ensure that this does not cause a surge in private sector insurance bills and regulators have to be ready to step in should private insurance discriminate on various medical grounds.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: This is especially as inflation in medical benefits is already expected to exceed inflation in healthcare post-subsidies.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Next, healthcare schemes and financing are currently extremely complex and are challenging for the person in the street to negotiate.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: For example, an individual in the sandwiched generation will have to understand the differences in schemes for both older and younger dependents.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: And if they buy IP riders, they will also need to understand the interaction between public and private healthcare for each dependent.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: In such situations, I hope that we can try and avoid situations where one ends up over-insuring their family in order to avoid the stress of being caught out unawares.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Apart from continuing to work on ensuring individuals feel secure about their ability to cope with the financial aspects associated with future healthcare costs, existing financial education efforts should target this specific point and address what families can do to avoid over-insuring, including demystifying complex insurance schemes which inevitably change from time to time due to developments in the macro environment.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: For those with low MediSave balances, the Government should offer more MediSave top-ups to address healthcare inflation while continuing to leverage its design which reduces wastage while cutting out-of-pocket costs for consumers.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: In this vein, we have to ensure that yearly MediSave withdrawal limits are updated yearly to reflect inflation, as medical costs can surge rapidly in a short period of time.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: At the time of the 2018 update, the $500 limit was enough to cover the average annual bill of a patient with three or more chronic conditions.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: However, we have to look to increase withdrawal limits to match healthcare inflation rates and consider allowing greater flexibility to use our MediSave savings.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: And this was also raised by Aljunied MP Gerald Giam in October last year.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: A third MediSave-related point is that our savings earmarked for healthcare expenditure could be used to better support mental health treatment.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Anecdotally, it appears that the wait times for access to counselling, therapy and other mental health care have driven some recipients to private services.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Alongside ongoing moves to grow public mental health services, can the Government consider allowing users to tap their own MediSave account for a range of private mental health treatments which would include psychotherapy, counselling and other forms of therapy like speech and occupational therapy?

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: This would mean bringing in practices run by therapists and other professionals to allow their treatment costs to also be covered by MediSave.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Mental health is no less important than physical health and poor mental health can lead to issues with physical health as well.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Since MediSave is already being approved for use for mental health services at places like Institute of Mental Health and polyclinics, I hope that we can consider expanding this to include the use of MediSave to access mental health services in other practice settings aside from purely psychiatric settings.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: This would be important to assist families from across the board, some of whom need to put in place early intervention strategies for their children's developmental issues, to support a multi-modal approach beyond psychiatric treatment to address neurodevelopmental, mental health conditions and symptoms.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: The WP, in our 2020 manifesto, called for there to be more subsidies for ILTC costs to relieve the out-of-pocket financial burden of social care for families who need it.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: With immediate cost of living pressures upon us, can the Ministry share details about the quantitative and qualitative impact the current cost of living crisis has had on the ability of households to pay for ILTC needs and what are the plans to ensure that they do not fall through the cracks and have to dial down on ILTC arrangements?

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: A next step in this revamp for subsidies would be to look again at related subsidies, for example, the Home Caregiving Grant that was brought up by Member for Hougang SMC Dennis Tan.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Additionally, it does not account for the loss of income or non-financial costs, such as the invisible workload associated with providing care at home for a family member.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: After all, what we put in our bodies will form a strong foundation for good physical and mental health.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: And by eating well, I do not mean swapping our national diet for the most expensive proteins or organic foods.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Eating well is eating in a way that at least meets what nutritionists recommend as a bare minimum.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: This is already contained in the Health Promotion Board (HPB)'s My Healthy Plate guide: a quarter whole grains, a quarter good sources of proteins, half fruit and vegetables.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: This, as many of us know, can be challenging to do, given our carbohydrate-dominant everyday cuisine.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: This is made even harder for those who work or live further away from supermarkets or places where there is a range of food options to facilitate a healthy diet and can be tough on those of us who work shifts.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: It is also harder to address rising food costs when many do not have access to a microwave or fridge at work, which makes it more difficult to bring healthier meals from home.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: The HPB has a Healthier Dining Programme encouraging availability and accessibility of healthier food and drink options across the island, but we can go further.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: For example, we can give more consideration and priority to stalls and restaurants that offer quantitatively healthier food under HDB's Price-Quality Method Tenders framework.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: We need to take steps now to help hard-working families already struggling to juggle their household balance sheets confidently deal with increases in the cost of care – health, preventative and social care – so that it does not become an insurmountable burden.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: With these in mind, I support the original Motion filed by the Leader of the Opposition.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Inflation and consequently elevated cost of living are very important issues.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: In the Labour Movement, this is a core concern that we have monitored closely over the years.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The effects are felt by all – workers, consumers and businesses.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Our older and lower wage workers would understandably be even more affected.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: During our "every worker matters" conversation concluded recently, more than half the workers aged 50 and above and workers at 20th percentile of income, felt that they were most impacted by the price of cooked food, groceries and utilities.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: This was exactly the items most susceptible to fall out from COVID, the Ukrainian-Russian war and other geopolitical events.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: With so much of our inflation being imported and affected by major global events, workers and residents often wonder what can be done.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Many of our workers and residents have already made lifestyle changes where possible by switching from eating out to cooking at home or by switching from private transport to public transport.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: With our workers taking action to manage cost, national policies have also helped our workers.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The Singapore dollar, as Mr Liang Eng Hwa has pointed out, is much stronger than many other currencies now.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: It is a fact not lost amongst our workers and residents who travelled in the region and beyond.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The Government is providing targeted support to cushion the impact of inflation, particularly for middle- to lower-income and retiree households.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The latter itself will cover 1.4 million older residents.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Our workers' common feedback is that there is just too many packages to remember, not that there are too many, but too many to remember.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: But these packages will ultimately be judged by its outcomes.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The Deputy Prime Minister also assured Parliament that the support measures combined will fully covered the increases in spending by the lower-income households this year, due to inflation and the GST rate increases and substantially cover the increases in spending by middle-income households.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: For our lower-wage and senior workers, the Prime Minister has announced at this year's National Day Rally that there will be further enhancement to the Workfare Incentive Scheme (WIS), Silver Support and matched retirement savings schemes, with details to be announced in 2024.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: These schemes, taken together, provide a good balance between cash and CPF MediSave savings, immediate and future needs.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: We need to deal with this current period of high inflation, but not forget the long-term structure challenges, such as the healthcare needs of an older population.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The Labour Movement stands ready to support our workers.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Cost of living issues should not be tackled by the Government alone.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: In NTUC, the FairPirce Group plays its time-honoured role to source and stockpile essential supplies for the nation.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: We can all remember how Singapore still had some goods on the shelves even in the deepest of COVID.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: It protects of people against price shocks experienced is so many other countries.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: FairPrice Group releases supplies on regular prices even if there are external global factors like logistics issues experienced during COVID that can cause huge upswings in prices.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: This can help to moderate domestic prices, especially during crisis.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The question is: what about the non-crisis time?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: NTUC is committed to helping Singaporeans meet this difficult inflation challenge.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: FairPrice, for example, has an extensive range of household brands too.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: They are priced at a minimum of 10% to 15% below comparable brands and quality.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: I know the aunties and uncles in my constituency, Tampines-Changkat, are very discriminating when it comes to prices and quality.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: They know exactly which days to shop for the best deals and we will welcome more of them to do that.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: But we will not rest on our laurels.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: In 2022, FairPrice started the "stretch a dollar" programme, giving a 5% discount on 100 essential items every Friday.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: At Kopitiam and FoodFare, prices of coffee and tea and the breakfast set were reduced or held constant throughout last year despite significant business cost increases.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: FairPrice and other social enterprises face the same cost pressures as any other commercial entities.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: So, those who use the FairPrice mobile app can also enjoy 10% off their meals at Kopitiam outlets island-wide.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: We note keenly that lower-income workers require the most help.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The Labour Movement charity and corporate philanthropy arms also provide support for low-income families and individuals.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Across areas, such as eldercare, education, community service, our social enterprises collectively dispersed about $12 million in 2022.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: NTUC certainly does not sit idly by but leans in to care for our workers and residents.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: On another front, just over the recent two months, the five Community Development Councils (CDCs) have launched a total of $40 million worth of funds to help residents cope with rising costs of living.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: This is in addition to the $600 million CDC vouchers that were issued island-wide over the past three years to support residents and small businesses.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The CDCs have put in place a wide range of assistance schemes to help low-income families with food, utilities education, transport, diapers, spectacles, mobility aides and more, with the new funds, for example.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: I will go through all the five CDCs.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Residents living Central Singapore can look forward to school bus fare subsidies, a neighbourhood job scheme, assistance for families with children living in rental flats.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Southwest residents will get more help for education, food, transportation and daily expenses.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Southeast residents will have a new EduCare fund to give additional help to low-income families, to students in primary and secondary schools.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Northwest residents will have a new support grant.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: We will focus on uplifting the least privileged, providing upscaling skills, connecting partners live in community.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Residents in the Northeast CDC would all have new internship mentoring opportunities, comprehensive financial support for school-going children.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Many thanks to the donors, partners and volunteers working with us on these initiatives.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: And there will be more to come for our residents.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: By coming together to work on programmes to uplift the less privilege and provide opportunities to the next generation, we not only help our families to combat inflation but also strengthen our social compact.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The examples of NTUC FairPrice Group and the CDC partnerships show that everyone can play a part in supporting one another to tide through difficult times.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: We can mitigate the impact of price increases and in doing so, strengthen our community.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: There is still more work to be done, but we can do so together.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Beyond the broad and many-stakeholders approach in solving our cost of living issues, the most important work is to keep wages ahead of inflation – real wage increase.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: No country can shield their citizens from cost issues in the longer term and do it sustainably.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: There are no quick workarounds with rising costs.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Many countries have resorted to things like price caps but only to abandon them when the bill size gets too monstrous.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The crux is to make sure that our workers can have real wage growth.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: This is where we must invest our resources, time and effort.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The key is a tight labour market and a productive workforce.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: A tight labour market gives workers bargaining power to command pay increases.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: We can keep it tight by continuing to bring in good quality investments that create jobs for Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Our policies have resulted in record levels of direct foreign investment commitments for the last three years – even more jobs for Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: We must continue to help our workers to secure good jobs.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: With no jobs, it can be worse than any inflation or inflation issues.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Together with Workforce Singapore and NTUC's e2i, we have strengthened our job placement.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: We have a Job Security Council to help our people get jobs, even in the deepest of COVID-19.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Recently, I visited a job fair organised by the Northeast CDC and e2i.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: There were 1,000 vacancies on offer, not as many jobseekers.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: I was secretly glad to hear from the employers that they found it difficult to hire locals and that they were improving their wages and workplace conditions to out-compete rivals.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: These are good signs for our local workers.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: A highly skilled workforce has been a cornerstone of Singapore's success and even more important in today's world, where skills are valued more than ever.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: This is not easy work because it takes years to get the policies right and see results.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The Industry Transformation Maps can provide that longer-term solution.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: At NTUC, we are glad that the Government is providing us with support to form Company Training Committees (CTCs).

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: These CTCs are now the backbone of many companies who are tranforming their businesses, with better wage outcomes for workers.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: We acknowledge that sustaining such real wage growth is immensely difficult, year on year.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: While we might not succeed every year, we must keep our focus on longer-term growth, for longer-term well-being.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: In providing real wage increases for our workers, we cannot do this alone.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: We work with our tripartite partners on the NWC to promote fair and sustainable wage increases.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: This year's NWC again demonstrates the resolve of tripartite partners to help workers cope with the cost-of-living increases.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Amidst increases in business costs, the NWC recommended a one-off payment, a lumpsum payment for all workers to cope with cost of living, with higher amounts for lower- to middle-income workers.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: What about our lower-wage workers – the ones who need more help?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: We have expanded the coverage of the Progressive Wage Model.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: NWC has also recommended increases in the Progressive Wage requirements for administrators and drivers.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: We are glad that our policies as a whole are working.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: There is already light at the end of the tunnel.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: We are continuing to extend our different packages of support and by keeping our workflow productive, we can sustain real wages and our quality of life.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: However, contrary to what the Member for Bukit Panjang seems to imply in his amendments to the Motion, domestic policy decisions like the hike in the GST, increases in water and electricity tariffs and rises in public transport fares, coupled with the skyrocketing cost of COEs, also contribute to the increase in the cost of living that Singaporeans are experiencing.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Blackbox Research's recent SensingSG survey found that 59% of Singapore residents highlighted cost of living among the two most important national and community issues.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Public transport costs are also a contributor to the cost of living in Singapore, making up 2.5% of MAS' core inflation basket.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Over the last 10 years, the rate of increase in bus and train fares has been faster than that of core inflation.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: This subsidy still does not eliminate the remaining 15.6% of fare increase, which the PTC has deferred to future reviews.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: In the meantime, public transport operators (PTOs) have continued to post eye watering profits.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: This is particularly jarring against the backdrop of increasing fares and Government subsidies.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: The PTOs and our current public transport model face little competition with each other because they operate different transport routes across the island.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Even duplications of the same routes for different transport modes are slowly being eliminated as bus services running parallel to new MRT lines are removed.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: These prompt questions about the efficacy of the current fare adjustment formula and a broader discussion around the sustainability of Singapore's public transport model.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: The current model consists of a mix of Government ownership of transport assets and operating contracts carved out among multiple profit-oriented PTOs.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: The model is inching more towards nationalisation than the Government would like to admit.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Starting in 2010, all real assets were transferred to the Government.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: The year 2012 saw the introduction of the $1.1 billion Bus Service Enhancement Plan.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: In 2013, the Bus Contracting Model saw bus services in certain areas tendered out to PTOs.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: The Land Transport Authority (LTA) now owns bus assets and pays the PTOs an operating fee while collecting all fare revenue and setting the service levels.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: This mesh of responsibilities involving the operators, the regulator and the Government potentially introduces inefficiencies and additional costs.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: These will eventually trickle down to commuters and taxpayers, manifesting in either increased fares, higher Government subsidies, lower service coverage or all of the above.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: In the past three years, about 30 bus services have been shortened or removed.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Such changes have affected my residents in Bedok Reservoir who continue to voice their concerns to me about long wait times and crowded feeder bus rides to the Bedok Mass Rapid Transit (MRT) station.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Elderly commuters who favour direct trunk services, which facilitate shorter walking distances for the commute, are also affected by these changes.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: This was first proposed by the WP in 2006.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: We envisaged the NTC as a publicly owned, nonprofit, multimodal land transport entity which will oversee the planning and operation of all MRT, Light Rapid Transit (LRT) and truck bus services in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: The NTC offers many benefits over the current public transport model.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: First, under the NTC, the substantial profits which go to PTOs and their shareholders could instead be redirected to benefit commuters.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Such revenue could mitigate fare increases and subsidise transport for the elderly, people with disabilities and low-income households, directly addressing concerns about the cost of living.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Second, with full access to the NTC's financial records, the Government could set fares just high enough to ensure the NTC's fiscal sustainability, without overly burdening commuters.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: The complex fare adjustment formula can be done away with.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Fare adjustments could be introduced progressively, avoiding abrupt changes during times of economic hardship.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Third, the NTC could manage bus interchanges, MRT and LRT stations and their associated linkways, leveraging the rent from these prime retail and commercial areas to support its operations.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: This will help moderate fare increases and the need for ever growing Government subsidies.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Fourth, the NTC could hire top transport engineers and managers, both locally and globally, based on their expertise, track records and commitment to public service.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Profit motives are not the sole drivers of efficiency and productivity improvements.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: By setting stringent key performance indicators (KPIs) and empowering these professionals, the NTC can continually improve service standards.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: The NTC's approach will see a marked improvement in performance management.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Sixth, a unified transport entity like the NTC would ensure more uniform service standards, enhanced service integration and comprehensive access to data for service improvement.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Utilising a vast array of commuter data, the NTC can employ artificial intelligence (AI) to forecast travel trends, dynamically directing buses and trains where they are most required.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Improvement suggested by commuters in one region of Singapore could be applied island-wide.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Seventh, the NTC would yield economies of scale in procurement, staff allocation and technological infrastructure, leading to further savings that benefit commuters.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Lastly, the NTC would be given the freedom to experiment with and spearhead land transport solutions and position Singapore at the vanguard of global transport innovations.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: This new model will place the needs and well-being of our commuters at the heart of our transport policy.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: It will not only address the immediate cost concerns of Singaporeans, but also steer Singapore's public transport into the future.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Speaker, Singapore has one of the lowest car ownership rates among advanced economies worldwide.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The upshot of this, is that our streets are amongst the least congested in the world compared to global cities such as London, Chicago or Paris, where drivers spend more than 130 hours in their cars, sitting in traffic in 2022.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Local commuters only lost 26 hours to jams and correspondingly less in terms of economic costs from lost time and petrol.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: This is admirable for a global city and one that we should not take for granted.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: This is evident for anyone who has had to endure rush hour in the major metropolitans of our neighbours, whether it be Bangkok, Kuala Lumpur, Jakarta or Manila.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The major reason for this favourable anomaly is, undoubtedly, the system of Electronic Road Pricing (ERP) and the Vehicle Quota System (VQS), of which, COEs are the much-reviled offshoot.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: This is one of the major drivers of ever-rising pressures on our nation's cost of living.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: And COEs were implicated in the most recent increase in headline inflation.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Some may argue that cars in Singapore are a luxury and a car-lite society is both better for the environment and more than made up for, by an excellent transportation system.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Surely, the price of COEs is only the concern of an elite few.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: But for middle-income families with younger children, as so many of my Sengkang residents are, a car is almost a necessity for getting kids to and from child care and school, co-curricular activities, enrichment class and weekend shopping trips.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Similarly, those who are elderly or less mobile may well feel that a car in the family is less of a luxury, and more of a need.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: And car ownership is more widespread than we may think; two in five households own one.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: And even for those who do not own a vehicle, the price of cars and COEs bleeds into our costs every time we hop into a taxi or book a private hire car.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The high prices of COEs for cars had even spilled over into that of motorcycles, at least until recently, where the relatively low costs of ownership used to be a refuge for those with more modest means wishing to have their own private mode of transport.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The VQS and COEs were introduced in 1990.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The objective, along with ERP, was to restrain ownership so that road traffic remains smooth.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Inherent in the policy is a decision to exchange certainty in congestion management, for uncertainty in prices faced by aspiring car owners, along with the possibility of inequity in access and usage.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Put another way, the Government consciously chose a quota system, knowing that it could lead to rising costs.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: If so, it follows then, that policy-makers should step in to manage prices when they get too far out of whack.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Since its introduction, the system has been repeatedly tweaked.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: These included minor adjustments, such as tenders became monthly instead of quarterly; but others have been more consequential, such as a decision to go from closed to open bidding, to make COEs non-transferable, or the collapsing of private-car categories into the present two.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: In 2018, the rate of growth of cars was frozen.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: This means that the stock of available COEs is now indefinitely fixed, and hence, the allocation of COEs is effectively zero-sum.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: If you are an aspiring car owner, but are priced out of the market, then too bad for you.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: If a well-off family can afford to buy multiple cars for each of their children, it will come at the expense of others who are less able to do so.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: This could be a delivery person who may need a vehicle for work, a household with a sick or disabled member that needs a car for routine hospital appointments, or a family of five who would benefit from one ride to shuttle their kids to and from school.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: But the Government has emphasised that – while it aims to keep COEs affordable – they were decidedly not a tool for enhancing progressivity.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: This capsule history lesson is instructive, because it helps us understand not only the motivations behind why a COE system was rolled out, but also, why this history has unwittingly introduced shackles that inhibits the successful and equitable functioning of the system today.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Perhaps the best way to think about COEs and the VQS is that it is a two-step system for controlling the vehicle population.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The VQS first sets the total number of cars that ply our roads.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: After this is established, bidding via COE efficiently allocates the available quotas to potential car owners.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: COE bidding requires each bidder to make offers, but only pay the price of the lowest successful offer.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: It was inspired by auction theory, and in particular, Nobel Prize winning insights into how best to ensure that each bidder bids as much as their own private valuations would carry them.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: At the same time, no bidder has any incentive to deviate from the bids that they put forward.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The outcome will, in theory, not only raise the same revenue as an auction awarded to the top bidder, but also allocate these COEs efficiently.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: This is all here and good, but herein lies the wrinkle between theory and practice.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: While the COE system was modeled after this so-called second-price, sealed-bid auction, real-world considerations have meant a departure from this theoretical ideal.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: There are multiple certificates to be issued, not just one.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: But these have had limited effect, which is unsurprising since the moves are one-off.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Measures that appeared to contain prices in the motorcycle COE markets are unlikely to work for car COEs, since dealer strategies for selling cars and motorbikes differ.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Perhaps most importantly, the freed COEs still constitute only a drop in the bucket of the overall quota shortfall relative to high-quota years.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Whereas a more decisive cut-and-paste is required to genuinely move the needle.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: To be clear, the Government is well aware of how relative quota differences are unequal across the years, and has been aware of this for a long time.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: In response to then-WP MP Mr Low Thia Khiang's query in 1998, about whether COE prices were due to such quota imbalances, then-Minister for Communications Mah Bow Tan simply explained that they were fixed at the beginning of each quota year, conveniently side-stepping the issue of whether a more balanced distribution of quotas were called for.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: A letter to The Straits Times on 14 October 2023 called for managing COE demand and supply, not alternative, newfangled systems.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Another online commenter to CNA claimed that we, and I quote, "are being penalised unnecessarily by a good system gone rogue".

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Transportation experts also expressed their displeasure that the COE system has not gone through a more fundamental review to deal with changes since being introduced 33 years ago.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: And unlike Vegas, what happens in the car COE market does not stay in the COE market.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Rising COE premiums affect the prices of used cars, of course.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: But they also affect the cost of motorcycles, which are frequently used not only for transport, but also to make a living.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: High COEs also add fuel to other expenses already on fire, ranging from private hire fees to motor repair.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Yet, in response to a PQs filed by the hon Member Mr Yip Hong Weng in 2022, the Ministry of Transport (MOT) stated that they would not be exercising any controls on the private hire car (PHC) market.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The response to another PQ filed by my hon friend Mr Louis Chua, likewise shunned the idea of restricting PHCs from the COE bidding process.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Indeed, the Ministry has gone as far as to say that "LTA has no plans to review the COE rules".

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: One approach, is to further segment the COE market in some way.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: This decision is not as radical as it seems.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Since the scheme was first introduced, there have been changes to the number of categories, before being continually refined to the present five as I mentioned earlier.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Today, there are routine calls to cater to separate, specialised categories of COEs.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: One way would be to drop the Open category altogether, or further tweak the criteria for the other categories.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: One could also create a category specifically for vehicles driven primarily for commercial purposes or, as I had suggested in my speech on the Electric Vehicles (EVs) Charging Bill late last year, for EVs.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: However, one potential implication of introducing additional categories is that, depending on the distribution of demand among the potential buyers, there could well be greater upward pressure on COE prices.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Overall, the evidence suggests that categorisation is often gamed, and as a result, would likely do little more to improve equity considerations. so, for me, it does not offer a substantive way forward, in terms of arresting price increases, even if it could be used to fulfil other objectives.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: One aggressive solution is to ban PHCs from the COE market entirely, managing their quotas separately.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: MOT has suggested that there is no evidence to support this argument and has even gone as far as to suggest that doing so, could even drive up costs for consumers.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Even so, it makes sense to remove PHCs from regular Category A (Cat A) and Cat B bidding.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: This is actually the current practice for taxi and cabs and given how PHCs essentially replicate many functions of the taxi – insofar as road usage is concerned – standardising the COE treatment for vehicles effectively used for commercial vehicles still makes eminent sense.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Of course, the practical question is how PHCs may be properly classified, if this were to be the case.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: I do not think that with rideshare data easily obtainable, that a data-savvy Government such as this cannot successfully make a determination between low-use PHCs – that is, cars that are only occasionally being operated as PHCs, when they do not exceeding a certain threshold of rides a month for instance – versus high-use PHCs, which are primarily operated as rideshare fleet cars.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: PHC drivers will be required to comply with their usage group, much like how weekend cars were restricted.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: And they will be monitored, by asking ride-hailing application companies to furnish these data.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Only high-use PHCs would then be required to bid in the Open category.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Another strategy is to alter the bid structure.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: One such suggestion – which has previously been rejected by the Government – is to pay for exactly what one bids, instead of the lowest successful bid.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Alternatively, bids could be set in terms of percentages of the open-market value of the vehicle.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: This system, the so-called ad valorem system, has been championed by some academics.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Relatedly, categorisations could be altered and pegged not to the, say, cubic capacity or engine horsepower, but market value.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Proposals of this nature are reasonable and have the added advantage of making the system more progressive.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: But, in my view, such proposals will make only a small dent on COE prices.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Importantly, this involves more than just the marginal transfers from expected de-registrations that are largely the focal point today.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: As mentioned earlier, the feast-and-famine nature of the COE market has long been recognised as a problem.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: We may even wish to reconsider transferability, since there is very little evidence that this practice actually increases speculation.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: But importantly, transferability should be allowed not to other car owners, but to other cars in the same category, for a given COE holder.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: This preserves the flexibility for car owners to sell early should their circumstances change, without introducing perverse incentives to game the system.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Thus far, I had focused mainly on supply-side proposals.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Hopefully, it should be clear that the enormous variation in COE prices has more to do with known and alterable supply factors, rather than demand, which the data suggests are secondary.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: But perhaps more importantly, demand effects should be expected to moderate even further in the future, since increases in per capita incomes – which alter structural demand growth – should already be expected to moderate, given how we have already attained the status as a high-income country.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: There is substantial evidence that speculators bid up COE prices.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Because dealers have a greater willingness to pass on costs – or occasionally absorb loss – they could contribute to upward price pressure, as some have suggested.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Others, to be fair, have argued that dealers have an incentive to keep COE bids low, since they sell cars and COEs in a bundle, and can pocket the difference if COE prices are low.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Regardless, the evidence suggests that dealer intermediation has likely resulted in greater concentration in the distributor industry, and such market power is seldom good for competitive prices.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: After all, price discovery has already improved substantially with open bidding, thereby diminishing some of the benefits of dealer hand-holding.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: In my view, the presence of distributors – despite the benefits of convenience of having a one-stop shop for purchasing a car – interferes enough with auction prices as to render their exclusion the lesser evil.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Better for such distributors to offer advisory and guidance, perhaps, for a fee, than be in a market-making position of collecting and making multiple bids.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The inequity of second or third car purchases has bothered many, and one proposal has been to apply some form of additional buyer duty on such purchases, as the Member Hazel Poa has mentioned, under the premise that these purchases – however small – could still fuel demand and push up COE prices, as my hon friend Gerald Giam has suggested.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: While the Ministry has declined to pursue such restrictions, one alternative – which admittedly would require some policing – would be to require households seeking a second or third car to do so in a distinct category, thereby limiting their price pressure on Cat A and B.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Even so, I will reiterate what my hon friend Faisal Manap had previously shared about our position on motorcycle COEs.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The issues in this category are somewhat distinct, not least because many riders are lower-income and require access not just for private transportation but to make a living.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Progressivity should, therefore, be an even greater concern in this market.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: More residents express anxiety and worry about affording daily living needs.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: As residents feel the pinch trying to cope with basic living expenditures, they start to worry about whether they can still support the broader needs of their loved ones and whether life aspirations, which have been spurring them on, are still within reach.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: These are valid concerns and we can all empathise very much.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Singapore is not alone in grappling with this issue of persistent rising cost of living.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Around the world, countries are witnessing similar trends.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Inflation rates are rising and the costs of essentials, such as food, energy and education, are soaring.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: The factors contributing to this trend are complex and multi-faceted.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: The COVID-19 pandemic has only exacerbated these challenges, with supply chain disruptions and increased public spending amplifying price pressures.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: As a small country with an open economy, we import most goods and, thus, have little influence over the prices set by others.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: While we have little influence over prices, our Government has the capability and duty to cushion the impact on our people and support Singaporeans through difficult times.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Ranging from sound fiscal policies, generous but targeted subsidies, purposeful support packages, quality education and skills training aligned to market needs, quality job creation, enabling competition to keep prices reasonable, to timely intervention to curb opportunistic profiteering, these are just some of the actions that our Government can and has taken over the years to help Singaporeans cope with cost of living.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
