text: I will not list the specific measures here, as fellow MPs have already highlighted them before, whether today or in past sessions, but I can share an example of how my resident, Mdm Ho, who is in her 40s, and her family have received Government support.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: The couple are working but do not earn much and, of the four children, one is in National Service, whilst three are still in school.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Hence, they struggle with cost of living, like any ordinary family in Singapore.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: In helping them to cope, the children receive various Government support, including MOE Financial Assistance that offered the youngest child, who is in Primary school, free textbooks, uniforms, meal vouchers and transport.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: The older schooling children receive meal vouchers and school bursaries, on top of the Edusave and CDA monies that they already have.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: The family also hold blue CHAS cards and receive full Medifund coverage, so, Mdm Ho and her two children are receiving regular medical treatments at no cost at Government restructured hospitals.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: In addition, up until Mdm Ho found a job earlier this year, the family also received public financial assistance from the Social Services Office.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: These public assistances are notwithstanding other Government support, such as the GST vouchers and Assurance packages.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Though Mdm Ho and her family have been receiving various types of Government support covering different needs, there are still moments when they needed a bit more help to make ends meet.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: So, we mobilised our own local help schemes in MacPherson to help them tide over.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: These include MacPherson’s utilities support scheme, S&CC support scheme, ComCare vouchers and local bursaries.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: These are fund-raised by our grassroots to give extra support to our residents and their families.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: I wanted to share this example because, in my opinion, the Government has been providing support to Singaporeans and families and actively responding to the evolving environment with targeted policies and programmes and that communities and individuals, too, can step in to cover last miles and close gaps.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: That being said, the recent intensity of escalating cost of living does necessitate our attention and actions.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Coming back to my earlier feedback about the increase in cooked food prices, I hope more support can be given to address it, given how fundamental and intrinsically intertwined hawker centres are with our daily lives.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: I should clarify that the price increase was despite the National Environment Agency (NEA) not increasing rent in most cases.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: In fact, for one of the hawker centres highlighted to me, there was rental reduction for some of the stalls.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: In MacPherson, most of the hawkers have been operating there for decades and share a strong bond with our residents, especially our seniors.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Hence, they make great efforts to absorb cost increments and avoid raising prices if they can help it.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: If I may warrant a guess, costs must have increased at every layer of their supply chain and the pile up was too much for our hawkers to bear.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Hence, there is scope for the Government to evaluate the impact further upstream and see how best to intervene, so that micro businesses like our hawkers can better manage their costs without being compelled to pass it on to the ordinary consumers.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Over the years, Singapore has maintained a prudent approach to fiscal planning, with a strong emphasis on balancing the Budget and ensuring sustainable economic growth.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Our Reserves also proved to be our most precious asset which saw us through the COVID-19 pandemic – the crisis of our generation.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Whilst there are obvious challenges that we still face, we have benefited from this Government’s policies in various ways.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: That being said, we must not undermine the stresses and hardships that ordinary Singaporeans face on a day-to-day basis.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: So, this Government must continue to pursue policies that will alleviate cost of living pressures on Singaporeans and families.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Looking ahead, against a challenging macro environment fraught with geopolitical instabilities and economic uncertainties, our Government must also continue pursuing policies that will build a future-ready Singapore and cultivate a resilient, versatile and capable Singaporean workforce, whilst ensuring future generations are free of burden so that they can soar high and live fully.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: (In Mandarin):   Mr Speaker, I support the Motion as amended by Member of Parliament Liang Eng Hwa.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: The amended Motion clearly reflects the challenges faced by Singapore and its citizens today, and more objectively reflects the reality of the global environment and the Government’s actual actions and intentions in the past, present and future.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: As the saying goes, clothing, food, housing and transportation are the basis of people’s survival and the people are the basis of survival of the country.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Clothing, food, housing and transportation are the most basic needs of the people.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Against the backdrop of fast-rising prices in recent years, it is understandable that our people are worried about the cost of living.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Macpherson is a mature estate with a majority of elderly and middle- to low-income residents.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Naturally, issues such as food, clothing and shelter have a greater impact on our residents.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: In the past year or so, in my conversations with residents, I have inevitably felt their pressure in terms of living expenses.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Although this is a common challenge faced by the world, for ordinary people, it is a matter of life and death that urgently needs to be resolved.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: In this regard, I believe that the Government will continue to pay attention to people's livelihoods, allocate funds and introduce targeted policies that are beneficial to the people to help them cope with various expenses.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: In addition to the Government's policies and various assistance programmes, the community, private enterprises and individuals can also show kindness and help those in need.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: For example, there is a 73-year-old Mdm Lim in our consistency.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: She is a cancer patient and is also the caregiver of her 90-year-old mother.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Under normal circumstances, the pressure in terms of living expenses is not small.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Therefore, the burden of the living expenses is lighter and the medical expenses are borne by the Government.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: In addition, we also provide them with assistance programmes and subsidise their other daily needs, and invite them to participate in welfare activities organised by our community partners.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: I do not know how many people have noticed, but I have an observation.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: In 2011, when I first became a Member of Parliament, I often heard elderly residents saying, in Singapore you can die, but you cannot get sick.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Shortly after, the Ministry of Health (MOH) introduced many policies to help Singaporeans, especially the elderly, to cope with medical and care expenses.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: In recent years, although I occasionally meet residents who are worried about medical expenses, I no longer hear the words "you can afford to die but cannot get sick".

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Of course, we cannot underestimate the pressures faced by Singaporeans.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: After all, the world is not peaceful and the global economic outlook is uncertain.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: We cannot predict how Singapore will be affected and what impacts it will have on Singaporeans.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Therefore, the Government must continue to monitor the situation and introduce policies that benefit the people.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: As an open economy with little natural resources, Singapore needs to import almost everything from abroad.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: In this situation, we are not price-setters and cannot control prices.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Some people may think that the Government should forcefully lower prices to benefit everyone, or that the present is more important and the Government can afford it, so it does not matter if we give more now, even if we borrow from future generations or we can use more Reserves.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: First, the idea of forcefully lowering prices is a one-size-fits-all approach.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Those who are economically able will consume more, which may lead to further price increases.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Then it is tantamount to drinking poison to quench thirst.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Second, the idea that it does not matter how much Reserves are used.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: As the saying goes, there is no perpetual good fortune and no hundred-day blooming flowers.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: The savings left by our predecessors helped us through the most difficult times.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Similarly, we must also consider the future of our descendants.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Our people do face many pressures and the Government must uphold the concept of people first and implement policies that are beneficial to the people and Singapore's long-term interests.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: I believe that the PAP Government will continue to care for the people and govern with the long-term welfare of the country and the people in mind.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: The impact has been especially severe on lower-income households, which I believe the Government is aware of.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: I welcome the support measures that have been announced to date towards alleviating some of these pressures, such as the top-ups to the payouts under the Assurance Package, the CDC Vouchers, the Public Transport Vouchers and so on.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: These measures are meant to bolster the existing social safety net.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: The social safety net which exists in Singapore is multi-layered, which the Government referred to previously as a "kueh lapis", with each layer meant to tackle a speciﬁc area of need.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: It is an approach meant to prevent dependency, free-riding and abuse of the various measures in place.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: I also note that Deputy Prime Minister Lawrence Wong had recently said that ComLink would be enhanced towards helping families in non-ﬁnancial ways, such as coaching.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: This is meant to aid social mobility and prevent further social stratiﬁcation.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: Having all these systems in place is well and good.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: However, I believe it is also important that we establish a means of assessing the eﬀectiveness of our social safety net.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: To this end, I would like to reiterate a call I ﬁrst made back in 2014 calling for Singapore to adopt the International Labour Organization (ILO)'s Social Protection Framework.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: ILO's social protection approach calls for a "fair and inclusive globalisation" involving an "integrated set of social policies designed to guarantee income security and access to essential social services for all, paying particular attention to vulnerable groups and protecting and empowering people across the life cycle".

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: There are four essential guarantees, namely, "access to essential healthcare for all, income security for children, assistance to vulnerable groups, and income security for the elderly and disabled." If the Government would prefer a more localised framework, then it is notable that a group of academics led by Assoc Prof Teo You Yenn and Dr Ng Kok Hoe have published two reports on the "Minimum Income Standard" for households in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: The latest version was released in September 2023 and provoked discussions in the media and online forums.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: The report has a comprehensive deﬁnition for what is considered a basic standard of living in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: It is about having opportunities in education, employment and work-life balance, and access to healthcare.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: A basic standard of living "enables a sense of belonging, respect, security and independence, and includes choices to participate in social activities and the freedom to engage in one's cultural and religious practices." In responding to the report, three Ministries, namely, MOF, MOM and MSF, released a joint statement.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: In that statement, they noted that what the report described was, I quote, "what individuals would like to have".

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: The Government also recapped the various measures that had been taken to address the needs of lower-income households, such as the payout increases for ComCare, the Progressive Wage Model and the Majulah Package.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: According to the statement, the Government, I quote, "regularly reviews the scope, coverage and the payout quanta of our schemes." I believe that the process of reviewing the various layers of social assistance can be further improved.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: Broadly, these levels do correspond to the existing thresholds for the Community Health Assist Scheme (CHAS).

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: There are several good reasons for establishing a more systematic approach towards tracking the eﬀectiveness of our social assistance programmes via the Social Protection Report.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: It would create accountability for the use of public funds in our social assistance programmes.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: Rather than report on spot ﬁgures on the numbers of recipient households, the report would present a more holistic picture on the state of social protection and assistance in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: The Government could also set objective KPIs based around the Social Protection Report.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: A vital KPI could be reducing the percentage of households in Steps 1 and 2 within a reasonable timeframe, perhaps within ﬁve years.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: If the percentages stagnate or if the report indicates a lack of progress, it could indicate a need to re-examine current approaches and identify gaps in the existing social protection system.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: For example, some recipient households may be in need of assistance in securing a place in a childcare centre or a student care centre for their primary school-aged children so that the parent can pursue employment without worrying about caregiving.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: The Social Protection Report could also be useful in raising awareness among Singaporeans of the nature of the issues faced by our lower-income groups.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: This, in turn, could foster better coordination between Voluntary Welfare Organisations (VWOs), non-governmental organisations (NGOs) and the Government agencies as they rely on a uniﬁed set of statistics and tracking tools.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: It may also encourage more individuals who are better oﬀ economically to step up and help their fellow Singaporeans in need by volunteering their time, energy or just making donations to aid the work of VWOs and NGOs.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: In 2014, I suggested that the Government adopt the social protection framework of the International Labour Organization.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: Through the framework, the Government is able to establish policies that guarantee income security and access to essential social services for everyone, giving special attention to the vulnerable group, and protecting and empowering our people throughout their life journey.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: There is also another framework in the report on Minimum Income Standard published by academics, Assoc Prof Teo You Yenn and Dr Ng Kok Hoe.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: With this information, we can better understand the effectiveness of the social assistance policies that exist in Singapore and also consider the need to change policies so that appropriate assistance can be provided for those in need.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: (In English): Sir, the Forward Singapore report that was recently released spoke of the risk of our society becoming more stratified and less mobile as our society develops.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: The Social Protection Framework I have proposed would complement the Government's effort to achieve this objective and track the progress of efforts undertaken towards achieving them.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Food and energy prices have risen significantly, caused by disruptions following Russia's invasion of Ukraine and extreme weather patterns.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: For instance, Germany saw natural gas prices peak in 2022, at nearly tenfold of the 2021 average.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: While prices have since moderated, they remain significantly above the pre-war prices.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: India continues to see prices spike across various food items, including essentials like rice and vegetables.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: From June to August this year, tomato prices surged by 1,400% at some wholesale markets.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: We have experienced price increases in Singapore, too.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: But we have to acknowledge that inflation has affected all Singaporeans.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Families need to spend more when they go to the market to buy groceries or when they have their meals in hawker centres and coffee shops.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: My residents in Bishan-Toa Payoh are affected, too, including lower-income families, retirees and couples with young children and elderly parents to support.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: As MPs and Grassroots Advisers, we understand the pain that our residents are going through, and we feel for them and their families.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: On top of imported inflation, we also face rising domestic cost pressures.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: We have a tight labour market and low levels of unemployment.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Real wages have been rising for workers across the board.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: We are committed to raising the income and skills of our lower-wage workers – something I trust Members from both sides of the House will support.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Through the Progressive Wage Model and other measures, the earnings of our lower-wage workers have increased faster than median wages.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: But wage growth means higher business costs, especially in more manpower-intensive sectors from healthcare to food services.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Right now, inflation has peaked and is on a broad moderating path.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: If we include the impact of the GST rate increase in January, core inflation for 2024 is projected at between 2.5% and 3.5%.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Fortunately, the impact of the GST increase is one-off.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: It should not cause an ongoing increase in the Consumer Price Index (CPI) in future years.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: These are positive signs, but the Government remains cautious because the global situation is uncertain and there are dark clouds on the horizon.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Further shocks to global energy and food prices could bring additional inflationary pressures and economic slowdown.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: There are many uncertainties in our external environment.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: But what is clear is this: the Government understands the concerns of Singaporeans and we stand ready to support Singaporeans where needed.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: First, MAS moved early to tighten monetary policy significantly, substantially strengthening the Singapore dollar.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: This has helped to contain imported inflation and preserve our international purchasing power.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Had we not done this, core inflation this year in 2023 would have been about 2.5 percentage points higher.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Second, we keep our economy competitive to create good jobs and sustain real income growth for Singaporeans.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Between 2017 and 2022, real median income grew by 1.8% per year.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Real income at the 20th percentile, that is, lower-income households, rose even faster, at 2.9% per year over the same period.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Unfortunately, in the first half of this year, median real income declined, even though nominal income rose slightly, as the Senior Minister of State for Manpower updated the House earlier today.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: This is due to the weaker economic outlook and elevated inflation.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: It is understandable for median real income to have ups and downs, depending on the overall economic performance.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: But our experience in Singapore is that so long as our economy grows and remains competitive, real income can continue increasing for a broad segment of our workers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: In the long run, the key to sustaining real wage growth is to raise productivity and upgrade the skills of our workforce, to take on better jobs with higher pay.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: The Government has invested in many initiatives to support businesses and workers in this transformation and we will continue to do so.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Third, we ensure that basic needs like education, healthcare, housing and public transport remain accessible and affordable for all.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Everyone receives some help in these areas, but those with less receive more support.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Even as inflation is moderating at the macro level, we recognise that many Singaporeans feel the pressures from higher costs of living.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: MPs from both sides of the House have raised this topic in Parliament, reflecting the concerns of our residents.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: To our fellow Singaporeans, the Government hears you and understands your worries.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: That is why we have been doing more to support Singaporeans, to cushion the impact of rising prices.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: We review our support regularly and step in to enhance it when necessary to provide additional support, especially for lower- and middle-income families.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: The Government enhanced the Assurance Package in Budget 2023.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: As Members will recall, 2022 saw the fastest rate of increase in prices since 2008, with consumer prices going up by 6.1%, compared to 2021.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: This way, we fulfilled our commitment to offset additional GST expenses for at least five years for the majority of Singaporean households and for about 10 years for the lower-income households.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Singaporeans will receive the additional support from these packages soon.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Every adult Singaporeans will get at least $200 in cash next month.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: And every Singaporean household will receive $500 in CDC vouchers in January 2024.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: HDB households will also get more help in U-Save and S&CC rebates.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Many of my residents, including retirees who are staying in private properties, said they appreciate the additional support provided and look forward to receiving the $800 special payment in December and the $500 CDC vouchers in January next year.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Through all of these packages, the Government will fully cover the increase in spending by lower-income households this year due to inflation and the GST and substantially cover the increase in spending by middle-income households.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: The Government provided this assurance at Budget 2023 and we will honour it.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: The broad-based support that we provide will help every family, but we recognise that there may still be gaps for some households.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: For families who need more help, we have other supporting measures, such as ComCare and the Silver Support Scheme.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: We will continue to monitor the trends closely.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: As we have often said, we are prepared to do more to support Singaporeans should it become necessary and we will do so in a manner which is fair, effective and sustainable for both current and future generations.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: The Government will continue to do our best to operate key services efficiently and keep costs of providing services as low as possible.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: In the case of water, PUB incorporates successful R&D efforts into its operations to reduce costs.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: For instance, the upcoming Tuas Water Reclamation Plant (Tuas WRP) will generate 80% of the energy it requires for used water treatment, compared to only 25% for the conventional WRPs.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: This will reduce energy costs and is made possible through enhanced primary treatment of used water and co-locating with the Integrated Waste Management Facility.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: But despite our best efforts, the cost of providing key services will be affected by rising inflation, including higher energy and manpower costs.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: So, the unavoidable question for us is how we want to pay for the cost increases.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: It is fair for these cost increases to be borne by the users and beneficiaries of these services – if not in full, at least partially, so that they are prudent in their usage.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: For example, when the cost of providing electricity or water goes up, we do want users to find ways to improve energy or water efficiency and to reduce their consumption.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Even as some of these cost increases are passed on to users, the Government is mindful that we must keep basic services affordable.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: For essential services like public healthcare, users only bear part of the cost.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: When costs go up, a large part of it is paid for by the Government through increased subsidies so that the bills facing users remain affordable.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: When fee increases cannot be avoided, we also provide targeted and direct support for more vulnerable groups in society, such as lower-income and retiree households.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Examples would include U-Save rebates and public transport vouchers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: But we need to remember that the cost increases do not magically disappear as a result.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: They still need to be paid for, whether by taxpayers today, or by our children and grandchildren in the future.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: We know from the experiences of other countries that subsidising petrol, electricity or water directly causes problems.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: First, it blunts the price signals and results in over-consumption because there is less incentive to improve efficiency and reduce wastage.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Second, households will get the subsidies whether they need them or not.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Furthermore, the wealthier segments of society are likely to end up getting the larger share of the subsidies, because they consume more.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: That is what happens when governments give out more subsidies for water and fuel.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: It is inevitably the higher-income groups with bigger homes and bigger cars, swimming pools and jacuzzis.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: So, the way we design our subsidies is important.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Instead of subsidising the services themselves or designing tiered pricing schemes, we price the services fully, but give direct help to households that need financial assistance, in cash or vouchers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: This way, we can target more help to lower- and middle-income Singaporeans.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: It is more cost effective and we can achieve better outcomes for society as a whole.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: I think Mr Pritam Singh would agree with me that water security is a matter of national survival.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Today, Singaporeans enjoy an uninterrupted supply of high-quality water.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: This did not come by accident, but is made possible by long-term planning, innovation and gumption.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Our founding Prime Minister Lee Kuan Yew famously said once: "every other policy has to bend at the knee for our water survival".

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: And that is precisely what happened – one of the most remarkable achievements in modern Singapore.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: We now have a sustainable and robust water supply system based on four National Taps.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: These are imported water from Johor, local catchments, NEWater and desalination.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Each of these taps plays a vital role in ensuring a safe and resilient water supply.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: But each of these taps also faces rising costs.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: To safeguard water security, we need to continue making investments to upgrade and maintain the system, while stewarding our limited resources.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Otherwise, the miracle that Mr Lee achieved will be short-lived.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Therefore, we must first right-price water to reflect its scarcity and to encourage its sustainable and prudent use.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: I was listening carefully to Mr Pritam Singh's speech earlier I do not think Mr Singh will disagree with me on this point.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Water is priced to recover the cost of its supply and production and to reflect the cost of producing the next drop of water from NEWater and desalination.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Even with active cost mitigation measures by Public Utilities Board (PUB), the total cost of supplying and producing water has increased significantly.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Singapore cannot compromise on having a high-quality and reliable water supply.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: It is necessary to revise the water price now to catch up with these cost increases.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Deferring the price increase now will only result in a widening cost gap, that has to be made up by larger, more significant price increases in future.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: As I mentioned earlier, we price water to reflect its scarcity value.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: This means the same rate is paid by everyone, from the very first drop used by the household, so that all users take into account the scarcity value of water.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: To discourage excessive use and to send a message to households on water conservation, we set a higher price for water consumption that far exceeds the average household consumption level.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: And as Mr Pritam Singh pointed out, this threshold is set at 40 cubic metres a month to accommodate most household needs.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Having additional tiers below 40 cubic metres would mean that all households, rich or poor, pay a water price lower than its scarcity value for the first block of consumption.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Or, if you have even more tiers, then, across the different tiers, the water that is being consumed at the lower tiers will also include a subsidy to the wealthier families that consume more water.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: This would distort the households' incentive to conserve water from the very first drop.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: It also means that the Government will have to subsidise everyone for water, not just the lower- and middle- income, which is more costly and inefficient.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Instead, the Government's approach is to price water fully.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Then, we provide targeted and tiered support though our U-Save rebates to those who need it most.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Lower-income families staying in smaller flats get a larger rebate, as I shared earlier, which effectively translates into a lower price for them.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: We do not subsidise their water or electricity consumption.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Instead, we work with them, including helping our SMEs to be more energy and water efficient.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: If the Government provides broad-based subsidies for all households through a multiple-tier water price, we cannot then also give out U-Save rebates for the same purpose.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: The experiences of other countries have shown clearly that broad-based subsidies can lead to wasteful and ineffective outcomes.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: The Government is unable, after spending on these subsidies, to have sufficient resources left to provide more targeted help to those who really need it.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: We have taken steps over the years to strengthen our energy resilience to ensure supply stability and continuity, and this is an important task that MTI, EMA and the power sector has taken on.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: The tariff, as Ms Sylvia Lim mentioned, should reflect the cost of producing electricity from the first electron.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Just as water, we want to price it correctly from the first drop.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: And then, what we do, similar to water, is we then provide means tested U-Save rebates to help families, especially lower- and middle-income families, give them more help, give them more support.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: And that is why MTI and EMA have also announced an initiative as Ms Lim had mentioned in her speech.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: This is an accurate reflection of the actual cost of producing electricity during different periods of the day.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Overall, we have provided high quality public services to Singaporeans and we have achieved good outcomes for our programmes, and we were able to do so, despite having an annual Budget that is less than 20% of Gross Domestic Product, which is much lower than most advanced economies.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Nevertheless, the Government's spending needs are rising steadily, especially healthcare costs as our society ages.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: There is therefore a need to raise revenues to pay for these higher expenditures.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: We have explained this in the House and also elsewhere many times.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: The Opposition has once again asked if we can defer the GST increase, especially given our higher-than-expected revenues.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: This too has been debated thoroughly in this House.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: I think it is important to set out once more the Government's philosophy behind the GST system.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: This includes rising social spending in areas such as increased healthcare for our ageing population and more support for vulnerable segments of society.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Second, we design our GST system to take care of the lower-income.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: In 2012, we made the GST voucher (GSTV) scheme permanent.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: The GSTV provides bigger offsets to lower-income households.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Coupled with the absorption of GST on publicly subsidised healthcare and education, we achieve an outcome where lower-income Singaporean households face a lower effective GST rate than higher-income ones.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: As we had shared in this House previously, the bulk of the GST revenues are paid by higher-income groups, as well as foreigners and tourists.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Third, we are able to defer the impact of the GST raises because of the comprehensive Assurance Package which benefits all Singaporean households.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: For lower-income households, we will defer the GST increase for them by about 10 years.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Since launching the Assurance Package in 2022, we have enhanced it twice to uphold this Government's commitment.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: And while the WP has consistently objected to the GST in previous years, we are glad that at the debate on the President's Address in April this year, the WP has acknowledged the need for a 7% GST.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: And earlier, I heard Mr Leong Mun Wai saying he also agrees with the 7% GST.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: But the WP and the PSP should be upfront and consistent.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: It cannot have it both ways, objecting each time the GST rate needs to go up, but wanting to keep and spend the revenues from previous GST increases.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: The only disagreement, based on my understanding that the Opposition now has, is to ask if we could defer the GST increase, because we have higher-than-expected revenues.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: We may have had a good year this FY, but we do not have a structural surplus.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Our fiscal expenditures have been rising steadily and will continue to increase and we are almost certain to face a funding gap in the coming years if we do nothing about it.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: MOF had published an Occasional Paper earlier this year to highlight this trend.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: We are expecting more social spending, in healthcare for our ageing population and to better support vulnerable groups in Singapore.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Without the GST increase and tax measures announced in the last two Budgets, we would not be able to close the projected fiscal gap.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: We have been fortunate to have higher-than-expected revenues in FY22.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: The Government did not plan its Budget on the basis that we will have these unexpected upsides in revenue collections.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: These were either sentiment-based revenues which are volatile from year-to-year, or due to higher-than-expected economic growth.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: And when we have these surpluses, the Government has made good use of them by flowing back these upsides to support businesses and households.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: We have done this during Budget and through off-Budget support packages.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: We can be confident that households will be amply cushioned by the Assurance Package, while we will have the higher GST rate in place, and can start to collect additional tax from non-citizens and visitors.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: I had mentioned this previously when we were discussing this issue, and I explained to Mr Giam and the House that we have to look at the different types of public transport service.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: For buses, for example, the revenue that is being collected from commuters does not go to the operators.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: The revenue comes to the Government, and the Government then pays the operators.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: We pay them a rate that was agreed through the bus contracting tenders.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: And I also shared with Mr Giam and the House that over time, as we gain experience in doing bus contracting, we had been able to squeeze out more productivity improvements and reduce the payments and the rate of return for the bus operators.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: For trains, the operators do collect fares to cover their operating costs, so the fares do affect their overall financials.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: And I shared, during October's Sitting, that in the latest financial year, after accounting for Government grants, SBS Transit reported a loss of several million dollars for their rail operations, while SMRT Trains reported an operating profit of $6 million dollars, which represents a profit margin of less than 1%.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: So, just to be very clear, these are the kind of returns for the rail operations.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: And I also shared what we are doing, an ongoing process to try and improve the way we do bus contracting, to be able to squeeze out more savings for commuters and taxpayers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Do we have a well-functioning public transport system overall?

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: So, from accessibility, affordability and also network improvements, system improvements, I think over time, our current system has achieved good outcomes for commuters, and this is also reflected in the overall survey results and ratings that commuters have given us.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Of course, I am not saying that there are no areas for improvement; there are, and we will continue to look at what we can do to improve.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: But overall, compared to many other cities, I think, to be fair to our public transport operators and to our public transport workers, who have been working very hard to achieve this outcomes, they have, overall, done a good job.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: So, what Mr Giam mentioned about nationalising, and I think he calls it the NTC, is actually not a silver bullet.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: I hope Mr Giam can agree with me that nationalising is not an assurance or guarantee that outcomes would be better.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Yes, you can take away the profit element if you nationalise and turn it into a Government department, but just because a nationalised entity does not make profits, does not make money, does not necessarily mean commuters will get better outcomes.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: I think we have to be quite clear about that.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: What we want, at the end, is to have better outcomes for commuters, to have a better transport system for Singapore.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: The then-Soviet Union, under the previous central planning system, uses KPIs to try and track performance, and I think that I do not have the elaborate further.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: I think Mr Giam will agree with me that it is not a good outcome.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: So, KPI is not a substitute for the profit motive that we need and the competition that we need, to spur the players to continuously improve.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: And we are adding additional pressure on them to improve their productivity.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: I understand, and I think I did explain this to him previously, that when we do some of the changes with the bus services, some of the commuters will be affected, and I do recognise that – my residents, too, have been affected by such changes.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: But the reason why we make these changes is because we have limited resources available to serve different needs, different groups of commuters.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: In different towns including, I am sure, Mr Giam's constituency, there will be new developments, new BTO flats, and the residents there will need new bus services to connect them to the bus interchange or to the MRT stations.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: So, where do we get the resources to serve these new demands?

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: We have to look at how can we re-allocate some of the existing services.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: We do not do it in a very drastic way because we do recognise the impact.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: We do it in a very calibrated manner, we look at which are the bus routes that run parallel to MRT lines, and where there is an option for people to take the bus, go to MRT station and then complete the longer part of their journey, the trunk service on the MRT.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: So, the bus then can provide better connectivity within the town as a feeder service.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: But having said that, I have mentioned this to Mr Giam before and I still make the offer to him today, if there are some specific areas of concern faced by his residents, please do let me know, please do let LTA colleagues know.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: And we will discuss with you to see what we can do to improve the situation on the ground.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: I want to start by saying that we just had a session on this yesterday.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: And I think Ms Hazel Poa and Assoc Prof Jamus Lim were both present in the Chamber.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: I do not know whether they heard my reply yesterday, because some of the points that they raised seem to have reflected that they heard me.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: But again, some of the points that they raised, they may have missed out or maybe they have forgotten what I have said.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: They are all the different fancy ideas for improving the COE system, that in the end, actually only make a small difference, or in his words "small dent".

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: We are going to do the "cut and fill" method, where we "cut" the supply from the peak years, and then we fill the troughs, the short-term trough years.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: So, by doing this, we are able to reduce the peak-to-trough ratio and achieve the outcome that I believe Assoc Prof Lim is also advocating for.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: But I also, in response to Mr Saktiandi, gave a qualifier that we cannot overdo this, because you are effectively borrowing supply from the future.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: These cars that we are now borrowing the COEs from, are still on the roads.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: We are doing that, but we also need to be mindful of the impact if we overdo it.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: But I do thank Assoc Prof Lim for actually agreeing with us, that this is the most effective way to be able to deal with these concerns that we see in the COE market.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: I mean, there is genuine demand for these cars, so you cannot just ban them.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: I think what he meant was to have a separate category that they do not have to participate in the COE bidding with the Cat A and B.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: We still have to look for where to re-allocate the supply of COEs to put into this new category.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: We are not talking about a magical solution, where I suddenly have new supply coming in.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: So, if we accept that point, Sir, then we are looking at a re-allocation from Cat A and B when we create this new category.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: And when we do that, as I explained yesterday, it is difficult to ascertain at what level of the supply should you shift into this new category, because the PHC market is still evolving and there are fluctuations from quarter to quarter, as we can see from the data.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: If you allocate too much, you shift too much, it will actually affect the supply of COEs in Cat A and Cat B, and that will cause prices to spike even further.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: I think Assoc Prof Lim understands this point.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: But if you do not allocate enough, you do not shift enough, then there could be a problem for the PHCs, and which will, in turn, affect the drivers and commuters.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: But they also serve a useful role in society, for commuters to meet their point-to-point journeys.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: This is not a closed bidding, where I do not know what people are bidding and I just go into the bid without knowing what other people are bidding.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: The COE system is online, you go in, you can see very clearly what other people are bidding, and you decide then how much you want to bid, based on your willingness to pay and you look at where that bid price is right now, and whether you are willing to pay more than that, to be able to secure the COE.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: So, whether we do pay-as-you-bid, or we do the current system, I think that the outcome will be the same.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: The second point that Assoc Prof Lim mentioned is, can we use open market value (OMV) instead of other criteria to determine the COE bidding?

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: It is not a perfect correlation, of course, but many of the cars in Cat A do have a lower OMV compared to the cars in Cat B, so I think to some extent, this already achieves that purpose of being progressive.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: But more importantly, Sir, we have the Additional Registration Fee (ARF).

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: I go back to my earlier point that Assoc Prof Lim mentioned as well, that he recognises that all these fanciful ideas are just going to have a small dent – in fact, I would say a very small dent – and this is not going to solve the fundamental issues.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: He agrees with us that the more fundamental approach, the better approach, is to look at how we can do more smoothening of the supply using the cut-and-fill method – which we are already doing.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Unfortunately, she is not in the Chamber right now.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Ms Poa asked whether we can have a 0.25% growth rate for Cat D.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: I think this is similar to the question that the Leader of the Opposition asked yesterday and Mr Murali Pillai also raised in November last year.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: As I had explained yesterday in the House, we have to look at the usage of motorcycles.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: It is similar to how PHCs are being used – because it can be dual use.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: People do use it for their personal use and also to do business, unlike, say, Cat C, where it is predominantly used for business needs.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: But I do acknowledge the concerns that Mr Pritam Singh, Mr Murali Pillai and Ms Hazel Poa have raised – which is that the buyers of motorcycles tend to come from more lower-income households compared to car buyers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: I had mentioned this in my reply yesterday.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: That is why we have lower ERP charges, we have lower ARF for motorcycles.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Ms Poa also asked about the point-based system.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: By this, I think what she meant is whether we can do the allocation by giving certain weightage to certain categories of families and buyers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: There are many Singapore families who would have a dependent, whether a young child or elderly parent.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: It would be very challenging to determine who is more deserving of a car.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: How would the person sitting at LTA be able to decide who is more deserving when all families would have different circumstances and needs?

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Instead, our approach is to make mass public transport affordable, accessible and convenient, and also to complement this with shared point-to-point transport services, including taxis, private hire vehicles and car sharing and through this multi-pronged approach, be able to better meet the needs of our Singaporean families, who may not need to own a car all the time and use it all the time but they may need it during certain times of the week to bring the family out for an outing or to send their parents for medical appointments.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: If we can create more options for them to be able to use the car without necessarily having to own the car, I think that is one way in which we can help more families.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: If you combine this with what I said earlier about the bidding system, they are not going to be the ones who are going to influence the bid price.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Likewise, families who own multiple cars – they make up 5% of the total number of resident households.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: So, again, the numbers are not so significant.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: We do not think that these two categories of buyers – foreigners and families that own multiple cars – will be the ones who actually end up driving the COE prices.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Because of that, introducing something like the ABSD may sound good, may make us feel "shiok" for short while, but it is not really going to solve the problem if our concern is about cost of living and high COE prices.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: It is not going to solve the problem.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: What Assoc Prof Lim mentioned earlier and what we are doing, the cut-and-fill, that is a more direct way of solving the problem.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: I think he may have misunderstood my data.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Maybe just allow me to clarify, Sir, that this trend has been happening not just in recent times when COE prices are high but even during the time when we have plentiful supply and COE prices were much lower.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Maybe more people now may not feel that driving is necessary.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Or like what I mentioned earlier, they may not need to own a car, they can just use the services of car from time to time when they need it.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: It could be that maybe they find that the public transport system has been improving over time and they would prefer to use public transport, which is also more sustainable for the environment.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Whichever the case may be, Sir, this trend has actually been consistent, whether COE prices are high or low.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: So, I thought I just clarify that point that Mr Leong mentioned.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Even in years when inflation is high, we still have to raise some charges and taxes because it is necessary to do so.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: It is not prudent or sustainable for the Government to avoid or subsidise every cost increase.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Doing so will entail either a high burden on current and future generations of taxpayers or a deterioration of service standards.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: It is not the responsible thing to keep kicking the can down the road or to avoid introducing painful but necessary increases.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: We may make some people happy by pursuing such policies but when the financing gap starts to accumulate over time, we will make everyone worse off because it will be even more painful to fix the problem later.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Importantly, the Government's policies should be seen together and not in isolation or piecemeal.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: The different policies and measures work together as a whole to collectively help ease the cost pressures on Singaporeans without undermining our fiscal sustainability.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: This is why I support the proposed amendment from Mr Liang Eng Hwa because he is right that the Government should continue pursuing policies that together lower cost of living pressures on Singaporeans and their families.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Our policies need to be sustainable because we care for Singaporeans now and also for our children and grandchildren.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: I also applaud and encourage the community and kind-hearted sponsors to continue stepping forward with philanthropic donations to help support vulnerable groups in society.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: There are many ground-up initiatives, including from the NTUC and community groups, which provide local-level assistance to vulnerable residents, on top of Government subsidies.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: You heard from some of our MPs earlier.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: The CDC Mayors and many of our grassroots advisers do this regularly with community partners and donors.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Community and corporations do their part alongside the Government in a whole-of-society effort to support the vulnerable.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: This is our Singapore way – not just enabling ourselves and our family to do well, but also helping to support others in society so that we can progress together and leave no one behind.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: We cannot fully insulate ourselves from these global forces.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Prices of goods and services will rise to reflect higher costs.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: If we do what is politically convenient and prevent prices from rising, I am afraid we will create more problems.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Giving more price subsidies will benefit certain groups at the expense of others.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: In particular, we end up helping the rich more than the poor.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: We will lose fiscal discipline and erode self-responsibility.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: The fiscal deficit that gets created cannot be wished away and the burden will fall on future generations of Singaporeans.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: In the long run, it will hurt Singapore and Singaporeans.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: We will continue to monitor the need for more targeted support if inflation or economic outlook worsens.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: We will do so while maintaining discipline in ensuring that our interventions are fair, sustainable and effective.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: The Government has been reviewing our policies, including as part of Forward Singapore.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance and Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Importantly, we will do this in a way that is responsible and right for Singaporeans, today and tomorrow.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: As I heard him, when he spoke about broad-based subsidies, I was concerned that he may have misunderstood my proposal.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: As we know, the price of water has three components.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: I had not been talking about the tariff and the waterborne fee.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: For example, the waterborne fee is a charge to offset the cost of treating used water and to maintain the public sewage system.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: When I spoke of tiers for water conservation tax, I was not suggesting that, for example, a user at 35 cubic metres per month is going to be charged zero to 10 at one rate, then 10 to 20 – once you hit 35, if you pay the water conservation tax, that would be tiered for users who consume between 30 and 40 cubic metres of water.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: That progressivity, in my view, would serve the purpose of the water conservation tax, which is to reinforce the water conservation message.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: The Acting Minister was talking about broad-based subsidies and the rich also getting subsidised.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: That was not the focus of what I was driving at.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: I will be happy to clarify if the Acting Minister has his queries on this.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: I think we are all on the same page when we want to look at how we mitigate the impact on lower-income families.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: The way that we are doing it now, all three components – the tariff, the water conservation tax and the water-borne fee – all three components actually add together to reflect the true cost of producing water, the next drop of water.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: And because of that, we feel that it is better to let this true cost be reflected from the first drop.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
