text: But then, we help the lower-income with means-tested U-Save rebates.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: But it is just the way in which we achieve it, we may differ somewhat.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: But I think, with Mr Pritam Singh's clarification, the gap has narrowed.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song
text: I am surprised that the Senior Minister of State is saying that setting KPIs does not work and he cited the Soviets.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song
text: Surely, he is aware that setting individual and team KPIs is an established practice in many organisations.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song
text: But my point was that tying an executive's salary to their achievement of performance targets is a better motivator of that executive's performance than a company's profitability.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song
text: It is also more aligned with commuters' interests.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song
text: Next, the Senior Minister of State said that with our NTC, there is no guarantee that it will get better outcomes.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song
text: But what we are seeing now is a public transport model that is sucking up Government subsidies while still posting million-dollar profits which benefit shareholders, not the commuters.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song
text: Can the Senior Minister of State then assure us that the current model is fiscally sustainable and will produce better outcomes in the long run?

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song
text: I was not criticising the public transport workers in any way.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song
text: In fact, I think they are doing a fantastic job in terms of keeping our public transport system working.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song
text: What I was talking about was the public transport model, not the workers.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: So, thank you to Mr Gerald Giam for acknowledging their hard work.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: So, if we look at SBST, for example, they have both local and overseas operations.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: SBST has MRT, bus and also overseas operations.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: So, if we take a look at the total package of the scope of what they do overall, I think those numbers would have to be looked at more specifically when it concerns the component that has to do with fares, because we are talking about fares here.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: So, there is no point we have an argument about how much money they make with their advertising or their overseas investments.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: It is part of the numbers that you see as a group.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: But for the purposes of our debate here, we should be looking at the numbers that are linked to fares.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: And as I explained earlier, Sir, for buses, yes, the profit numbers today that you see reflect some of the older contracts that we did previously.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: But if we look at the newer contracts, we have, with experience, actually tightened the terms and conditions.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: So, as a process, achieving savings for commuters and for taxpayers, that will take time to achieve, but we are making steps in the right direction.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: We are seeing a reduction in the returns for the newer contracts.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: For MRT, I need to highlight that what we are talking about here again — I am sorry, Sir, just to reiterate one more point on the bus is that the fares do not go to the bus operators directly.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: So, if we collect less than what we have to pay them, that is actually Government subsidy.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: So, I think we have to look at it in the right perspective rather than look at the macro numbers, which may not be relevant to the discussion that we are currently having with public transport fares.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: On the second point about KPIs, Sir, I did not say that KPIs are not relevant at all.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: What I said was that KPIs should not be a substitute, because if you only rely on KPIs and nothing else, then you will have a problem.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: But I do not think that is what Mr Gerald Giam is saying as well.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: I think we can both agree that KPIs can form part of the overall performance management tracking, but they should not be the only way of improving performance.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: And in the case of the public transport operations, if we look at buses, for example, one of the reasons why we are able to have better outcomes, partly, I want to give credit to our LTA colleagues.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: It is because, over time, we do learn how to do the contracting better.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: But it is also because there is more competition.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: So, if you nationalise, you take away this competition element, you may not actually achieve the same outcomes as what you are able to achieve now.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: It is an assumption that nationalising, taking away the profit element, means better outcomes for commuters.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: The first has to do what Senior Minister of State Chee mentioned.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: He said he wondered if I heard him yesterday.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: And that is why I referred to the cut-and-fill method.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: But I also wonder if he heard me just now when I also pointed out that the Government action in the cut-and-fill method did not strike me as decisive enough.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: And if they are willing to do so, how will they actually avoid the existing incentives for individuals to sell COEs in shortage years and to buy them in abundant years.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: The second one has to do with what the Senior Minister of State mentioned about PHC participation in Cat E.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: So, I did hear the suggestion from Assoc Prof Jamus Lim.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Same concept but the Member wants us to do more.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: And I clarified that it is not that we do not want to do more but there are trade-offs and we need to be careful because, if you borrow too much, you actually may introduce more volatility.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Please do not forget that the cars that are being deregistered in future, some of them may want to buy another car.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: And we are also borrowing from the future.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: So, you are effectively shifting some of the supply to now before the cars are deregistered.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: So, you are adding to the short-term congestion.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: So, yes, we accept those trade-offs and we are willing to do some, but to what extent?

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: But the more important point is that we do not disagree on the method.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: We both agree that cut-and-fill to reduce the peak and trough is the more effective way.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: If I may add, Sir, on PHCs, because that is the second question from Assoc Prof Jamus Lim.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: That number is actually more than for the previous few quarters the percentage of car-leasing companies that were bidding.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: So, if you look at the companies that are bidding PHCs, I shared yesterday that, for Cat A, it is about 21% or thereabouts, it dropped to 16% in the last quarter.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Of course, I did qualify that I cannot predict how prices will move because that depends on demand, and demand is not within the Government's control.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: But in terms of planning and injecting, we are doing our best to try and inject as much as we can without affecting the future supply volatility and without affecting short-term congestion on the roads.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: But whether you treat it like taxis or you put it as a separate category, that means, different from taxis, the reality is that you still need supply to come from somewhere, right?

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: You cannot just suddenly have new supply magically appear.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: It will be Cat A and Cat B.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: So, if you create a new category, whether you put it together with taxis or you put it separately, you have to move some of the existing supply from Cat A and Cat B to this new category.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: It is not that it is undoable or unthinkable but it introduces complexities because we run the risk of either over re-allocating or under re-allocating and that would have unintended consequences.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: I have one clarification for the Acting Minister.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: Does he not agree that when we talk about utilities in the current climate, conservation is a key aspect of it.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: We have seen recent statements about the need to conserve energy and water.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: In this respect, U-Save vouchers, no doubt they are appreciated by the residents who receive them, but it actually does not really encourage conservation of the utilities.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: So, I am just wondering whether the Acting Minister would agree that we may have to keep an open mind as to whether we need further tools to encourage residents to conserve on the use of utilities.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: If we look at it from the recipient's point of view, this is a fixed amount, means-tested.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: But what they receive is a fixed amount.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: If they consume a lot, actually, the amount of subsidies they receive is still the same.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: If they consume less, then actually, the amount of subsidies can help them to sometimes even fully offset the electricity bill or to reduce it substantially.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: In our case, we reflect fully the price so as we incentivise the right behaviour to conserve electricity and water, a point that we both agree.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: But the way in which we then provide the help is through the U-Save rebates.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: It does not change the incentive to want to conserve, but it provides the help in a means-tested manner to our lower- and middle-income families.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: First, the Senior Minister of State mentioned that the bus fare goes to LTA, not to the bus operators.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Can I clarify then who proposes the revision in bus fares?

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Second, I thank the Senior Minister of State for responding to my suggestions about the points-based system.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: He mentioned that it would be difficult because there are many families with children and, therefore, a bit difficult to decide.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Would he consider a system whereby, say, the bidding price is given a certain number of points, say, every $1,000 is one point, and then every child that the family has is allocated a certain number of points, so that those with more children get more points and those families with people with disabilities (PwDs) also get additional points?

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: And then COEs are allocated based on the total number of points.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The Senior Minister of State mentioned the Disabled Persons Scheme (DPS), which I understand is only for livelihood purposes, not for families with disabled people, and for them to move around.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: In October, I shared the fare formula and that was also previously announced, and the different components that made up this fare formula.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: There are some indicators that we look at – what is the national benchmark for wage increases, what is the CPI, what is the energy cost.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: And, of course, as I mentioned earlier, there is that productivity component to incentivise the operators to want to improve productivity over time.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: You cannot run away from some judgement call if you go down a points system because who would be more deserving?

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: It is really going to be very, very difficult to differentiate.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: If you use the number of children, for example, I have four children, but I think Ms Poa will agree I should not get additional subsidies or priority just because I have four children.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: So, there are many, many situations that you look at; it is very difficult to then say how many children as the only yardstick or as the only criterion.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: So, the way that we think about it is this: how do we help the families through different avenues – not just COE alone, because COE is really more for allocation of a scarce resource – but how do we help different families who may need the car not all the time, but at certain times of the day or certain times of the week.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: So, one way is to use point-to-point service, and we are doing a review on that; a point-to-point review.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: How do we enhance the services for commuters to meet evolving commuter needs?

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: And it will include families that Ms Poa and others have highlighted, where there is a genuine need for point-to-point service and instead of just relying on car ownership alone.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Some of them can own a car but some of them may not be able to own a car.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Point-to-point service, car sharing, and I think it takes a whole-of-society approach, not just the Government because for many of these families that need help, sometimes they also receive some help from the community and from voluntary welfare organisations (VWOs).

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: So, it is a whole-of-society effort; that we do our best to support these families.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Ms Lim, do you have a further clarification?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: But as I hear the debate go on, I just felt that probably it is about balance.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: So, I would like to ask the Acting Minister two questions with regard to that.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I think the way the Government conducts policies today, a lot is profit-seeking and using the market model.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: So, I think, as the alternative parties, what we are bringing to the House is that we hear a lot of feedback about problems.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: So, the angle must be, besides using the market model completely, there must be more consideration for the social aspects of a lot of the policies.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: So, let me ask the Acting Minister two questions in relation to that.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We know from the statistics provided by the Government that most of the increase in the water demand comes from the big users – the water-intensive industries and all that.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: So, maybe the Government wants to make ourselves more competitive —

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Mr Leong, you should just ask your clarification and not make another speech.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: So, we want to know whether if we alter the way the water is priced, the Leader of Opposition talked about having another category under 40 cubic metres.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: Is it possible to have another category, between 40 cubic metres and 80 cubic metres, so that we differentiate and we push the cost more to the big users?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: Because right now, you look at the water prices we are doing and whenever we need to increase our water supply, we need investments.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: And so, as a result, the burden of the investments comes back to the average Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: Second point about the COE, it is the same thing.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: But if we use the market system, the Singaporeans will be squeezed out of the market very soon, the average Singaporean.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: So, as a result, do you agree that we ought to see how we allocate this scarce supply of cars, not just by the market price but by the Government coming in?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: Maybe one of the solutions, do you agree, is to adjust the allocation to, like what I said in my speech, those that go to Cat B, shrink it; increase the supply for Cat A and C drastically.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: Currently, I think it is about 50/50, right?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: Will that solve the problem? "Solve the problem" meaning, will that allow average Singaporeans a better chance of having a car, even going into the future?

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: I just spent a good 40 to 45 minutes explaining our approach to helping Singaporeans cope with the rising cost of living and what we are doing through different ways in a fair, effective and sustainable manner.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: We can discuss different possibilities, like what the Leader of Opposition and I have done just now on water.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Can I pause here to ask if the Member agrees to withdraw that comment first before I answer the rest of his questions.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: So, if they want to ensure that the public services are profitable, then it is profit-seeking.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: So, if there are certain industries like the bus services that you cannot make a profit yet, then it might be because that you are still trying out the model.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: Because this contracting is a new model, when compared to other things.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: But whereas in the established areas, like water and COE, you definitely have —

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Mr Leong, actually all Senior Minister of State Chee is asking is: are you withdrawing?

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: If you are not, then the short answer is no.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: But in the interest of time, maybe just allow me to comment on one thing.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Because they meet the needs of our residents.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Because they meet the connectivity, commuting needs of Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: So, even when the bus service is not making money, we know this is a public good.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: So, Sir, we are looking for financially and fiscally sustainable outcomes.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: If you listen to different generations of Finance Ministers during Budget, there will always be one segment on the economy because we do need to grow the economy to earn a living, to create jobs.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: But there is always an important segment also on social policies.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: National Day Rally – the Prime Minister has always focused as well on different ways of improving our social policies – housing, education, healthcare.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: So, again, Sir, I reject the way that Mr Leong has characterised the Government's way of working to say that we only care about profits and there is no social aspect in our policymaking.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: He said that we should have a different category from 40 cubic metres to 80 cubic metres.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: So, I am a bit puzzled why Mr Leong is proposing that we should have a different category between 40 cubic metres to 80 cubic metres, catering to some of this 4% and then to provide subsidies for them.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: I find it quite strange why he is proposing something like this.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: I thought the right thing to do, Sir, is to price the water correctly from the first drop, starting from the first drop.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: But we understand that there are different families with different needs, different financial circumstances and we want to then provide more help and support to the lower- and middle-income families.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: And the way to do this, the most effective way, in our view, is to then provide means-tested U-Save rebates that are fixed in a the quantity, so that if you consume more, actually beyond that, you pay.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: So, there is a strong element, strong incentive to encourage people to save water.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: I think that is the better way to do it and not to create a new category between 40 cubic metres to 80 cubic metres.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: But we are just trying to clarify further.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: So, can I reply to the Acting Minister through you, that one, I did not say that the Government did not consider social factors at all.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: What I am saying is that, when we are debating here, maybe we are trying to push and say that, let us consider the social factors a bit more?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: So, as a result, I think the Acting Minister has also misunderstood me.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: What I mean to say is that for water, for example, the water demand is increasing very fast but it is because of the big user.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: So, recently, when we announced the 18% increase in water price, if we have another category for the bigger user, then maybe the lowest 40 cubic metres do not need to have price increases.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: Push the price increase to the next category.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: Of course, it will affect the competitiveness of the water-intensive businesses in Singapore but it is unfair for Singaporeans, right?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: When the big users are the ones who are increasing the demand and we have to put a lot of investment into water supply and then the costs are borne by the smaller user because of the price increase.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: So, when we look at businesses, we charge them the full price of water from the first drop and we do not give them any U-Save rebates unlike households.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: What we do with them is to help them to improve their energy and water efficiency.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Mr Leong, if it is a clarification, I will allow it.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa
text: I like to seek a clarification from Senior Minister of State when he said that the bus services are making losses, can I clarify whether that takes into account advertising revenue from advertising on the bus surface, the panels behind the bus, in the bus, panels at the bus stop, at the bus interchanges, rent from kiosks at the bus stops, at the bus interchanges and so on?

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: I do not know which advertising firm Ms Poa has in mind but if you think you can make $1 billion dollars in advertising revenue, please let me know.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Mr Leong, if it is a clarification, yes.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: One more clarification for the Senior Minister of State.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: As far as I know from the statistics, currently the big users account for 55% of the demand, right?

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: I need to go back and double check this.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: (In Malay):   I am concerned about the rising cost of living that our people are experiencing.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: There will also be rebates to manage Service & Conservancy Charges (S&CC) and U-Save rebates.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Some of the inflationary pressures that Singaporeans are facing are also happening worldwide, due to the Russia-Ukraine war and bad harvests related to climate change, for example, driving up energy and food prices.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Not to mention the risks of supply chain disruptions, higher interest rates in a longer environment and the possibility of an escalation of the situation in the Middle East.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Aside from specific government support through fiscal assistance, which have been very helpful to our people, many Singaporeans may not know that our government and financial agencies actually play a big part in shielding their wallets from some of these economic spillovers.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: While inflation is still elevated, MAS' five successive monetary policy tightening moves since October 2021 have tempered the momentum of price increases.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The effects of MAS' monetary policy tightening are still working through the economy and should dampen inflation even further.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I am also concerned and have asked many questions alongside other Members in the House about the increase in transport costs including high COE for motorcycles and cars.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The Government recognises that some Singaporeans and the Malay-Muslim community rely on motorcycles for their livelihood, and there is a higher proportion of lower-income individuals among motorcycle owners than car owners.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: This is one of the reasons why the ARS Additional Registration Charges, road tax and Electronic Road Pricing (ERP) for motorcycles are lower than other types of vehicles.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: To protect against speculative bidding behaviour for Category D COEs, MOT introduced several measures in the last two years.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: It includes raising the bid deposit for Category D Temporary COEs, or TCOEs, to $1,500; and reducing the validity period of COEs to one month.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The Government has said it will continue to study ways to improve the COE system for Category D, including new ideas.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Hence, I am waiting whether they will look at ways to improve this system.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: (In English): Sir, some of the inflationary pressures that Singaporeans are facing are worldwide – I mentioned this in my Malay segment – due to the Russia-Ukraine war and bad harvests related to climate change, for example, driving up energy and food prices.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I think many are not aware – I mentioned in my Malay segment about how MAS policy has helped to mitigate imported inflation.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: According to a study by NUS, Singapore’s food prices are also much less volatile than global food prices.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: This in part is due again to our exchange rate policy accordingly and is helping us in terms of purchasing power in the world market, thereby, providing a greater buffer towards global food price shocks.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: As cited by the NUS study, our various policies such as increased local production, diversification of food sources and stockpiling are all working to help insulate Singaporeans from externally driven cost of living pressures, albeit the cost of living pressures continued to be there because of global factors.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The issuance of CDC Vouchers to households is of special mention – I mentioned it in my Malay segment as well – these are complemented at the local level by individual constituencies’ grassroots efforts.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I think Acting Minister Chee highlighted that in his speech as well as other Members as well.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I just want to share the experience at Toa Payoh East, at the local level, for example, I launched the Cost of Living Assistance Programme, called CLAP, sometime in the third quarter of 2022, a ground-up initiative working together with hawkers and donors and grassroots to assist lower- to lower-middle income households – we wanted to capture the lower-middle income households – in Toa Payoh East with their daily expenses.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Ground-up initiatives with the merchants and grassroots supported initiatives to assist residents who are affected by high cost of living especially groceries and essentials.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I just want to highlight, it is a tripartite involvement – merchants, residents and Toa Payoh East Citizens’ Consultative Committees (CCC) – to help residents as much as possible and also to make sure that the hawkers actually do have business.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: This initiative also hopes to bring back some business opportunities to the heartland shops and convenience for residents.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: So, they get about $100 worth of CLAP vouchers, which can be used to offset their purchase for meals and essentials items at the participating hawkers and heartland merchants.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The purpose I am sharing this is to highlight that there are discretionary measures that advisers and MPs can do on top of the ComCare and welfare assistance that are available that the Government has provided to alleviate cost pressures which includes CDC Vouchers, GST rebates and transport vouchers.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I am wanting to highlight that the CDC Vouchers are not means-tested.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: It is the Government spending about $600 million, I think, if I am not mistaken – up to about $600 million so far and is not means-tested.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: So, on top of that, we have these discretionary measures that, I think, all the advisers and MPs can undertake in their respective constituencies.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Against this global backdrop, Mr Speaker, the Government is also implementing tough decisions for longer-term economic policies and fiscal measures.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Acting Minister Chee has highlighted extensively the impact of the increases in the GST and how they matter for Singapore – carbon tax and water prices, COE quotas, for example, with specific objectives.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The main thing is it helps to ensure long-term fiscal sustainability and reduces burdening future generations of Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: These are necessary to achieve other policy objectives beyond just keeping inflationary pressures for Singaporeans' day-to-day lives in check.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: It is essential that Singapore continues to address our medium- to long-term challenges head on even as we face inflationary challenges now.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: That is the Singaporean way, and I think Acting Minister Chee mentioned it, that has ensured Singapore’s survival, gelling a very long-term strategic perspective even as we face short-term challenges but with the welfare of Singaporeans taken care of and negative impact mitigated, especially for the more vulnerable groups.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: These policies will invariably lead to price increases in the short term, but ensure fiscal sustainability and environmental sustainability measures are needed now and I think we need to address them now before things get worse in the medium to long term.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: All these are already mentioned by Members as well as Acting Minister Chee earlier.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: One example I just want to highlight again, as what the Acting Minister has mentioned, is the recent announcement by the Public Transport Council to allow a 7% fare increase in 2023.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: This is one example reiterating again what the Acting Minister mentioned, one instance where the Government has calibrated the impact of cost of living pressures.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The Acting Minister for Transport has also explained the recent decisions and the Government's core consideration that fares remain affordable while the public transport system remains financially sustainable.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: These further measures accompanying the fare increases demonstrate the Government's approach to targeted help in ameliorating cost of living pressures for the lower-income group.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: In general, I am reassured in terms of public transport, that the Government has kept public transport fares affordable.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The Government is actually spending quite extensively with the additional subsidies to lower the proportion of household income spent on public transport, which has fallen as well.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Before I go into my last segment and conclude, I just want to reiterate some feedback from residents, highlighting thanks in terms of efforts from MOT and LTA in providing those transport vouchers to residents.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Many of the residents have come forward to seek help in terms of transport vouchers.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I think that sort of additional help on that front has helped, especially with the recent changes in the monthly passes as well.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Another example I want to highlight before I end is the additional U-Save rebates announced last month that will serve to cushion the impact of increases in carbon tax and water price.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: This is another way that the Government is making sure that the cost of living pressures on the lower-income households are moderated even when we need to make the hard decisions of implementing such policies at this juncture.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Ultimately, the global inflationary environment and pressing needs from Singapore society, such as an ageing population, mean that there are multiple fiscal demands that the Singapore Government needs to meet.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: As a society, we will all need to take on a fair share of these cost pressures where the Government will ensure that it is affordable for the average Singaporean while taking special targeted measures to provide more assistance for the lower-income groups who have heavier financial burdens.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: There is no guarantee that we may already have shifted into a new normal of higher prices.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: In this vein, there may not come a better time to implement some of these policies.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Food and food ingredient prices have gone up by 11%.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: For F&B establishments, including hawker centres, coffee shops and restaurants, prices have gone up by 12.5%.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Many residents have told me that the extent and speed of cost-of-living price increases have become unbearable.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Previously, you can buy a lot of things with $50 at the wet market, but now it does not buy you much.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: As Members of Parliament, we feel keenly the impact of cost of living on Singaporeans in the past two years.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Thus, today's debate is of great significance and precisely because of this, our debate should stick to the facts and analyse the factors behind the rise in cost of living objectively and accurately, and take a realistic approach to alleviate concerns of Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: This includes various considerations, trade-offs and compromise so as to avoid politicising this issue.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: This is the responsibility that Members of Parliament and political leaders should take upon themselves.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: The first point I want to make is that GST should not be made the scapegoat of the increase in prices.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: A crucial point is that the Government has increased the subsidies for the lowest-income Singaporeans under the permanent GST Voucher scheme.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: This will fully offset the impact of GST increase on the 30% lowest-income Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: This means that the actual impact of GST increase on these Singaporeans is not two percentage points, but zero.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Even for middle-income Singaporeans, the actual impact of the GST increase is also much lower than one percentage point.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Because the Government boldly launched the Assurance Package, the impact will only be felt five to 10 years later.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: This means that the cost-of-living pressure that Singaporeans are experiencing now is due to other reasons, not GST.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: One key reason is the global market volatility and the rise in global prices.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Singapore is a small country and we import many of our raw materials and goods, so we will be inevitably affected by fluctuations in global prices.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: For example, global chicken feed price has increased in the past two years.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: So, we have experienced an increase in egg and chicken prices.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Global oil and gas prices have also increased and directly affected our electricity price, MRT fare and prices of public services.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: As a small country, what can we do?

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: The Government has one major weapon, which is the Singapore dollar.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: I believe Singaporeans know that the strength of the Singapore dollar did not occur by chance.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: It is due to the Government's prudent management of the economy and finance.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Individually, we can also take steps to cope.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: In fact, a lot of residents know that domestic prices are affected by the global market.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Singaporeans can also take a prudent approach in spending.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: When we talk about inflation, it is actually an aggregate of the price increases of all goods, but in this basket of goods, there are still cheaper choices available.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: According to official data, average prices of red snapper and batang have indeed increased by 20% and we have seen this at the markets.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: But according to official data, the price of sea bass has remained stable during the same period.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: So, we can eat sea bass instead of red snapper and batang.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Savvy saver are still able to save money.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Another important aspect is the increase in the prices of public services.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: The cost of public services is also affected by the global market and prices.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: For the increase in cost, the Government has chosen to increase prices to maintain high quality public services.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: For Town Councils, although they are not Government departments, they also provide public services.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Thus, the recent increase in Town Council S&CC charges also reflects these increases in cost.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: This is a responsible way to deal with cost increases.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Besides the global market, another factor for the increase in the cost of living is our domestic wages.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: In particular, I would like to point out the increase in the wages of low-income Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Increasing the wages of low-income Singaporeans is the aim of the Government's Progressive Wage Model (PWM).

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: This is higher than the 1.8% annual wage increase of middle-income workers.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: In the next five years, the Government will go one step further and aim to increase the wages of low-wage Singaporeans by up to 80%.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: This will benefit hundreds of thousands low-wage Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Sustaining this wage increase of low-income workers at a faster pace than middle-income workers so as to close the gap between the two is something that the Government has put a lot of effort into.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: As a Jurong GRC Member of Parliament, many of my residents have benefited from the PWM.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: So, I strongly support this policy, but this policy also implies that the overall domestic wage will increase and ultimately businesses will have to increase prices.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: A crucial consideration is whether Singaporeans support the PWM and whether they are willing to pay a little more so that low-income workers can earn more.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Hawkers are self-employed persons, so they are not included in the PWM, but they also work hard to make a living.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Hawker food prices have increased not just because food and electricity prices have increased.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: I have a resident who runs a noodle stall.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: I asked him, "So, you have increased your prices." He said, "I have no choice." What I was hesitant to ask was, actually, "Others have increased prices and you are only increasing prices now?" So, Singaporeans have to face the same question.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Are we willing to pay a little more at hawker centres so that hawkers can earn a little more?

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: This reflects the fundamental policy of the Government, that is, a small country will always face big challenges.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: When we are faced with challenges, the Government faces the problem squarely and launches responsible and sustainable policies as there is no free lunch in the world.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: The Government will directly bear part of the cost, while the rest is shared with the people.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: In the past, we have faced similar challenges and the current issue of cost of living is no exception.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: In fact, many Singaporeans are aware of this.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Many residents have asked me, "The Government is providing so much assistance.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: How can it be sustained?" As long as the Government, people and business community continue to work closely together and contribute their part, I believe we can overcome the current challenge of cost of living.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: I support the amended Motion by Mr Liang Eng Hwa.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: The discussion on the cost of living crisis which we are facing today, is not complete without a review on the state of inflation in the country.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: In recent months, we have seen inflation rates gradually slowing down over the course of the year.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: The decline in overall inflation rates is perhaps cold comfort for many Singaporeans, as prices are ultimately continuing to rise even amid the high prices we are seeing today.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: And that this is still significantly higher than what we have been used to in Singapore, double that of the 1% to 2% average inflation rates in the last four decades.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Even if inflation rates return to lower levels, prices are now permanently higher.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: With crude prices rising meaningfully since the third quarter, potentially even hitting $150 as the World Bank has warned, food commodities prices threatening to climb even higher if we witness a strong El Niño, and the second order effects on inflation potentially coming through, inflationary pressures could well pick up.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Interestingly, the MAS expects core inflation to be lower than headline inflation at 2.5% to 3.5% for the year as a whole.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Unlike many countries where core inflation is defined as that excluding food and energy costs, Singapore excludes accommodation and private road transport costs, which according to the MAS, and I quote, “are excluded as they tend to be significantly influenced by supply-side administrative policies and are volatile.” While I accept that the MAS Core Inflation measure is used for monetary policy decisions, a person without knowledge of the technicalities will nonetheless find reports of a return to price stability as being different compared to their lived experience.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: After all, the CPI is meant to be a fixed basket of goods and services commonly consumed by resident households.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: And looking at the relative weight of accommodation cost as part of Singapore's CPI basket, it comes in at 21.97% – the highest single component.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Moreover, to say that accommodation costs have no direct impact on the monthly cash expenditure of most households in Singapore as they already own their homes, does not take away the fact that especially in a country like ours, which prioritises home ownership.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: The cost of purchasing a home is a big concern, as it is going to be the single largest expenditure item for the vast majority of households.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: It is not just any expenditure item, but one that relates to our basic need of providing for shelter and our livelihoods.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: As such, my speech today will primarily touch on housing, and as rightly pointed out by the MAS, is significantly influenced by supply-side administrative policies.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Hence, we need to take a closer look at our supply-side policies to ensure prices are well managed.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Before I touch on housing, back to the October Monetary Policy Statement.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: The MAS took pains to reiterate that excluding the impact of the increase in GST rates both in 2023 and 2024, inflation rates would be lower.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: The question then is, why add fuel to fire?

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Layering on a higher GST rate on top of the inflationary environment we see today with the rising prices of many essential goods and services, is only going to make it even more difficult for Singaporeans to cope with the mounting cost of living pressures.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Should we not be insulating our people instead of hitting them with more?

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Even the MAS Chief Mr Ravi Menon has acknowledged the 1% dish point increase in GST, has an immediate impact on inflation.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: This is especially the case where I shared in my speech in Parliament just last month: the Government's fiscal position is shaping out to be much better than projected, with operating revenues now $8.2 billion higher in the first half of the financial year.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: To reiterate, in Budget 2022, Deputy Prime Minister Lawrence Wong shared that the GST hike will bring in about 0.7% of GDP in revenues annually, or about $3.5 billion when the full hike is in place in 2024.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: In response to my speech, Senior Minister of State Chee Hong Tat repeated the same response as that shared by Deputy Prime Minister Lawrence Wong in the Budget 2023 round-up speech, where according to them both, “Deferring the GST increase will only store up more problems for the future, leaving us with less resources to take care of our growing fiscal needs and we cannot count on short-term upsides to fund structural needs.” Again, I listen very carefully to what Senior Minister of State Chee has said earlier, but the question here remains relevant.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: And that is, is deferring the GST hike in 2024, even for one year, when we have already achieved the revenue increase which the GST hike was meant to bring, going to store up more problems for the future?

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Returning to the subject of my speech today, which is on housing costs.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Compared to a year ago, public housing prices are now 6% higher versus private housing prices at about 4% higher.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Moreover, it is not like what a Business Times columnist puts it, where he calls on Singaporeans to simply "stay cool and do not go overboard chasing after million-dollar HDB flats".

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: While one may argue that the HDB resale market does not reflect the affordability of new BTO flats, ultimately, this will feed directly into the formula for pricing new BTO flats, as Minister Desmond Lee shared that, and I quote, "When pricing new flats, HDB first establishes their market value by considering the prices of comparable resale flats nearby as well as the individual attributes of the flats, and prevailing market conditions." Looking at the residential rental market, Minister Desmond Lee is hopeful that in the coming quarters, rental pressures are expected to further ease, as a significant number of residential units are completed, as shared in response to a PQ in September where Member Mr Henry Kwek asked, what more can the Ministry do to moderate or reverse escalating rental cost to help tenants manage their cost of living.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: While the HDB does not publish a rental index, a comparison of median rentals across HDB towns paints a similar uncomfortable picture.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Over the last three years, median rents for a 4-room HDB flat have risen by roughly 35% to 78%.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: While we may say that as a country with close to 90% home ownership rate, those who need to rent form a minority.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Soaring rents impact young Singaporeans who have not been able to purchase a flat but need their own space and households who may be particularly vulnerable given their tight financial circumstances and yet do not qualify for a public rental flat as they may be earning a household income of more than $1,500 a month, for example.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: I am cognisant that the HDB website has recently been updated to remove references to any income figure and that HDB takes a needs-based approach and reviews all requests for public rental holistically.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: The ability to afford other housing options, such as renting from the open market or purchasing a flat remains debatable, in my view.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: This is especially if households are currently renting in the open market, and cannot afford the high resale prices today.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Even if some can eventually secure a BTO flat, they would need a place to call home in the interim.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Just last month, there were two separate residents who lamented to me that their landlord is raising their rent to beyond their gross household income.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: In one case, his rent is going up from $1,500 to $2,500 a month, beyond his gross income of $2,200 a month; while in another case, his rent is going up from $3,200 to $4,200 a month and he cannot simply downgrade to a smaller flat due to his household size of eight.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: I have in January and March 2023, called for support measures for households in need and these cases are just a small subset of many Singaporeans who face similar predicaments.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Having described the challenges we are facing in the public housing market, I recognise that the Government agrees that there are issues relating to availability and affordability today.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Where I believe our views differ however, is on the sufficiency of the current measures that have been taken.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: On housing availability, the Government has reiterated its position that it has significantly increased the supply of BTO flats and will launch up to 100,000 new flats in total from 2021 to 2025.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Similarly, I have over the course of a number of speeches, shared that this may not be sufficient.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Even if the HDB launches 100,000 flats in total from 2021 to 2025, this implies that BTO supply falls 20% from current levels to about 18,400 flats in 2024 and 2025.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Moreover, while BTO application rates have in 2023 declined to about three times thus far, it remains unclear if the 1.6 times application rate seen in the October BTO exercise is sustainable, or just a result of the first-time introduction of certain specific rules.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: On housing affordability in Budget 2023, the Government has increased the CPF Housing Grant for first-time families to enhance housing affordability in the resale market.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: As what a head of research at one of the real estate agencies pointed out then, such beneficial effects could be short-lived as it could result in further price inflation, as these could be priced in by the market.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: In addition, with the new BTO classification system from second half 2024, Plus flats will be priced with more subsidies, on top of the subsidies already provided for standard flats today.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Again, while the intention is to improve affordability, with the new classification applying only to new BTO launches and not to the existing stock of more than a million HDB units already in the market, the measures could potentially add further upside pressure to resale HDB prices in some of these locations.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: As reported by CNA last month, prices for flats located near MRT stations or town centres are now higher by up to $10,000 compared to before, according to industry insiders.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Moreover, there has not been any concrete policy proposals on addressing the needs of those needing to rent in the open market.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: In response to my Parliamentary Question (PQ) in January 2023, Minister Desmond Lee shared that, "Providing subsidies or grants for renting flats in the open market is likely to induce demand and drive up market rents, which would compound rather than help solve matters.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: As such, we have no plans to provide such rental subsidies".

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Is this not the exact approach that the Government is taking, when providing targeted subsidies to enhance affordability in the resale market?

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Especially when it comes to vulnerable families who have not been able to obtain a public rental flat?

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: What then should be done to address the issues of availability and affordability today?

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: To put simply, if the fundamental demand-supply imbalance we are seeing today is not sufficiently addressed, the market is simply doing what it is supposed to do.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: With prices and rents continuing to appreciate, while many Singaporeans are not able to address their housing needs.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: If the idea is not to crimp the real demand side of the equation since access to appropriate housing and shelter is a basic need for all, addressing these problems would then necessarily require adjustments to the supply side of the equation, for the market to find a more appropriate equilibrium point.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: In other words, we need to increase the supply of HDB flats across both the for-purchase market and also the neglected for-rent market.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: As I have shared in my MND Committee of Supply speech, a local academic put it very succinctly, and I quote, “Having excess flats is actually a feature and not a bug.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: It just means that if some Singaporean want to get married and wants a new house straight away, there is a house available!” And he goes on further to say, “To me, BTO is the real culprit behind our uncontrolled fire”.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Moreover, a lot of the demand from first time home buyers in the resale market today is also a function of the long wait times for a new BTO flat.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: To take it one step further from ensuring adequate supply, we ought to also ensure that we strive to continue reducing the long waiting times for a BTO flat and build a larger percentage of flats ahead of demand, as I have shared in my MND Committee of Supply speeches over the years.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: After all, if we can build industrial facilities ahead of demand, can we not also build residential homes ahead of demand and have a fundamental re-think of the BTO system?

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: I do appreciate Minister Desmond Lee's assurance that the HDB is planning to launch more Shorter Waiting Time flats, of around 2,000 to 3,000 flats per year by 2025.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: However, this is essentially at similar levels to the number of such flats launched in the last five years, ranging from about 1,096 in 2018 to 2,850 in 2020.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: In the rental market, it is alarming that while there continues to be a very limited stock of rental flats today, the pace of construction appears to be slowing drastically compared to before.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: That appears to be a noticeable slowdown compared to the average net increase of 1,640 units per year between 2011 and 2020.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: In other words, just about 180 flats per year.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Why are we constructing new rental flats at a pace which is a mere 10% of that in the past decade?

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: To minimise the agonising wait for an allocation of a rental flat and to alleviate the worries of many Singaporeans who have not been able to access a rental flat, it is imperative that we do not neglect the housing needs of vulnerable Singaporeans in our pursuit of home ownership as the only acceptable housing model for Singapore.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: And it is important for us to resume the pace of rental flat construction, to be at least on par with the net increase between 2011 and 2020.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: This could partly explain the tightness we are seeing in the housing market today.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: And while I am not privy to the Government's desired population growth rate, if such growth rates persist, then we could have an even bigger problem down the line with housing supply set to taper off from next year.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: The lease decay issue continues to be the elephant in the room, and more than five years since the term "VERS" entered our lexicon in Prime Minister Lee's National Day Rally speech in 2018, many unanswered questions remain.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: (In Mandarin):   Although the inflation rate has eased in the recent months, prices remain high and continued to be on the rise for many Singaporeans, and the current inflation rate is still much higher than what we were used to.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Regarding public housing, the latest data shows that as of June 2023, Singapore's population has grown by 5% to reach 5.92 million.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: This is the fastest growth rate since 2008.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Last year, the number of registered marriages also reached an all-time high in our country's history.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: To effectively address the housing problem, we need to adjust the housing supply, so that the market can find a more suitable equilibrium.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: In other words, we need to increase the supply in the BTO market, as well as the rental market which has been overlooked.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: We are now rebuilding our communities, our businesses and our trade links.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: This is a mammoth task made even more complicated with the ongoing wars.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: As we traverse the new world in the new normal, and as we pick up pieces – broken families, familiar places now gone, groups dispersed – we find ourselves in the middle of a hurricane of cost increases and resource shortages.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: From petrol, electricity and water, to bus rides, cai png and kopi – indeed, the global cost increases are felt at very local, very personal and very real everyday ways.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: In Punggol, a town of young families, many with upwardly aspirations, my residents have shared with me their concerns over food prices, healthcare costs, utilities and tuition enrichment classes for their children and, of course, the cost of owning a car and property in Singapore.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: They have expressed their appreciation for GST Vouchers, CDC Vouchers, U-Save Vouchers, Transport Vouchers, bursaries and top-ups that they have received over the years to help with cost pressures.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: For some residents who have fallen on tough times post-COVID-19, perhaps from being retrenched, a business gone south or having fallen gravely ill, help is never too far away with SSO, CDCs, Medical Social Workers.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: For those who have somehow fallen through the cracks – a single parent, a caregiver wishing to return to work, an undiagnosed special needs adult, our local community welfare teams provide weekly ration packs, monthly essential items, care vouchers and pro-bono services, like legal clinics, respite care and counselling sessions.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Our Town Council, too, has also formalised a welfare committee assisting residents who have fallen behind on their S&CC fees or needing simple repairs around their homes.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Support, of all shapes and sizes, are readily available and always at hand.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: And yet, in Punggol, I have observed that there are more who are stepping up to support the community instead.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Indeed, when the going gets tough, the tough gets going!

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Complementing national level policies, micro-spheres of influence make long-term, impactful differences on the ground.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Our micro-spheres of merchants, small businesses, religious organisations, volunteer groups and charities have created a sustainable and wide web of safety nets for our residents.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: I am touched that our temples, themselves reeling from low temple donations during COVID-19, now provide weekly rations to my welfare team, packed full of nutritious goodies to be distributed to our residents.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Our temples, churches and mosques give free Maths and Language tuition for our residents, and they doubled their classes post-COVID-19 when demand surged.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: A moral welfare society is now building a free traditional chinese medicine (TCM) clinic to complement primary care in Punggol.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: All residents across all households and age groups are welcome.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Many volunteers at the tuition and TCM centres are retired educators and healthcare professionals, and I appreciate how Singaporeans stepping up to support their communities.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: With all these examples, I do believe in our businesses and community ecosystems – to do right for themselves and for our community – in the face of challenges and pressures, finding the right balance between costs of living and costs of business.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Perhaps, instead of looking at this as a tug of war, let us support and help our businesses, our SMEs, our towkays do something that they do best in, and that is selling their goods and services well, and creating good jobs, future-ready good jobs.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: The Labour Movement supports our companies with the upskilling of their workers and the redesign of jobs, so that more pockets of workers – such as caregivers, women returners – can partake in the workforce, and alleviate income pressures at home.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: An example of such a programme is the C U Back at Work, or CUB, Programme that the NTUC Woman and Family Unit has piloted to help mothers and family caregivers to return to the workplace confidently.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Flexible Work Arrangements (FWAs) is key to the program, and companies redesign work hours or locations around the time availability of workers.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Instead of price cuts and the passing on of costs to just another stakeholder upstream or downstream, FWAs can solve financial stresses for Singaporean families by adding an extra channel of income and help companies with resources and productivity.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Hence, Mr Speaker, let us help our Singapore businesses do better in what they have set out to do.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: I call on our Government to reduce business costs by simplifying work and Government compliance processes for our businesses, and to support our companies in job redesign and the upskilling of workers.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: And indeed, in the face of global price surges and its impact on everyday life of Singaporeans, I have seen the mettle in our Singaporean businesses, I have felt the kindness in our communities and I have heard the steely timbre in our people's voices.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: Acting Minister Chee had earlier shared in detail on how we tackle rising costs – managing the Singapore dollar to contain imported inflation, ensuring our economy remains competitive to create good jobs and sustain real income growth, and providing support packages targeted especially for vulnerable groups.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: I wish to respond to some specific points raised by Members on topics including housing affordability, cooked food prices and profiteering.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: Members would recall we have had an extensive debate in this Chamber in February on housing affordability and even more recently, there was a major announcement on upcoming changes to the BTO classification framework.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: Before I respond to points made by Members, including Mr Louis Chua and Mr Leong Mun Wai, please allow me to set out the Government's overall approach towards maintaining stability in the housing market.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: As economic conditions improve and wages rise in Singapore over the long term, we expect to see this reflected in a gradual rise in housing values and prices.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: Sudden shocks in either the public or private housing markets will cause serious problems and even hardship for Singaporeans, and this is why the Government actively uses policy levers to moderate price increases.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: First, careful land use planning, coupled with a land recycling strategy, to ensure a steady supply of both public and private housing, to meet Singaporeans' needs.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: Second, pricing BTOs, which by the way, in response to the point made about the five "C"s, these BTOs have become more and more similar to condominiums, in terms of build quality and aesthetics.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: Pricing these BTOs with a view to affordability, not cost recovery.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: Third, demand-side levers for public housing such as grants and priority schemes for various categories of buyers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: Fourth, maintaining controls on home loan financing, whether through CPF or cash to encourage prudence on the part of home buyers and moderate price increases in the HDB resale and private property markets.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: And fifth, additional measures such as ABSD to cool the overall housing market where necessary.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: Recent housing price movements have been due to specific imbalances which the Government has identified.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: The first imbalance: our building programme fell behind in the last three years due to COVID and we are catching up.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: The resumption of delivery of private housing will also, over time, ease the crunch in private housing and moderate rentals and home prices.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: HDB resale prices have risen significantly in recent years.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: This is due to buyers turning to resale when BTO construction was affected by COVID-related delays and shifts in social norms prompted by the experience of the pandemic, contributing to overall increase in housing demand.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: Coupled with the broader economic climate and mortgage interest rate increases, these have moderated property prices.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: The prices of private residential properties increased by 0.8% in 3Q2023, lower than the quarterly average of 2.1% in 2022.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: Similarly, prices of HDB resale flats increased by 1.3% in 3Q2023, a figure that I believe Mr Louis Chua also quoted just now.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: And this is lower than the quarterly average of 2.5% in 2022.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: This is the fact that mature estate BTOs had presented a specific set of concerns.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: The price of mature estate BTOs drove much of the ground concern about BTO prices.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: So, when people talked about BTO prices being a concern, they were mostly talking about the BTO prices that they saw in the mature estates.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: The issue we faced was how to price mature estate BTOs because these are very sought after so that they do not rise out of reach of most buyers and also not in a way that induces its own demand, which is why we announced the introduction of a new housing framework, comprising a new classification of "Standard", "Plus" and "Prime" flats, to take effect from the second half of 2024 onwards.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: The new framework seeks to ensure homeownership remains affordable, including in choice areas, by providing additional subsidies to these flats, but also tighter restrictions, so that they are affordable even upon resale.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: This also helps to keep our system of subsidies fair, while keeping to market principles.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: This means that we can also maintain a good social mix, even in good locations, because housing will be accessible to a wider range of Singaporeans.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: Based on our ground engagements, Singaporeans are generally aware of and support the new housing framework and its objectives.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: This will help implementation go more smoothly next year.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: So, measures are in place for each of the specific imbalances causing price increases in BTO, resale and the private housing markets.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: Despite having to tackle these imbalances, we have broadly maintained measures of public housing affordability.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: This meant that they could finance their monthly instalment with CPF, with little to no cash outlay.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: The Government will continue to monitor closely and adjust policies whenever necessary.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: And I am glad that Mr Louis Chua acknowledges our housing moves.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: However, he seems to think that we have not done enough.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: I noticed that Mr Louis Chua had co-authored a piece in January this year, saying housing in Singapore is affordable.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: But I am glad that he agrees that the fundamental issue with housing affordability is one of supply, not policy.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: But we are catching up with the backlog.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: Mr Louis Chua seems to think we should build more.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: In fact, HDB is already doing all it can on the supply side.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: We have also activated more levers on the demand side, for instance, by prioritising BTO flats for young married couples.
